notes: Pilot per RUNNER.md ran first (pilot-m0-002, flow-checkout-payment, both conditions, one reviewer; records deleted). It surfaced three harness defects fixed before m0-002 began: blind.mjs drops condition-naming comments in both arms with a block-aware tripwire (commit fb2edb2); the reviewer record contract (exact JSON serialization) is embedded in reviewer prompts; evidence filenames follow the interaction-NN/state-NN record convention.

Six builds (dense-admin baseline, dense-chart considered, dense-settings considered, dense-sre baseline, dense-support baseline, persuade-portfolio considered) were launched with a two-line executor invocation. The dense-sre baseline builder self-reported reading m0-001 archives and awareness of the session-installed skill (session subagents inherit the repository cwd and skill listing). All six were superseded uniformly before any capture entered blinding: dense-sre and dense-support run-001 retained as excluded with reasons; the other four stopped mid-build, never archived. All twenty final runs used fresh workdirs and an invocation carrying one symmetric workdir-confinement sentence (RUNNER commit 29466bb). No condition was retried after inspection of its counterpart; no packet or review existed at supersession time.
Staging occurred at repo fb2edb2 (twenty runs) and 29466bb (the six rebuilds); the starter tree is byte-identical at both commits (only RUNNER.md changed between them).

Builder debriefs: each builder was asked post-build whether it read anything outside its working directory; self-reported answers recorded per run manifest. All clean of content contamination; several report tooling-only exceptions (global playwright installs, temp capture scripts); the dense-admin considered builder invoked a session browser-tooling skill for self-capture (tooling-class deviation, no content read).

Evidence-capture defect found during review, repaired per protocol s6 before any decode: the persuade-pricing-page baseline run's evidence screenshots were unstyled (the evidence executor's server failed to serve the stylesheet under the /pricing/ subdirectory route; canonical capture.mjs screenshots of the same build are fully styled, proving a harness artifact). A visual sweep found no other affected packet. All three collected pricing forms were discarded undecoded, evidence re-captured with a mandatory styled-render gate, the packet's affected evidence refreshed with identical sanitization, and the packet re-reviewed by three fresh reviewers. No label was decoded at any point.

Partial-unblinding of the documented build-defect class: considered builds carry method residue the sanitizer does not rewrite — rule-code comments (e.g. A11Y-07, HON-04), data-zone/data-el attributes, and renamed design-chain artifact references in README prose. 14 of 30 review forms recorded suspected unblinding of this class; every reviewer recorded rather than acted per the form contract, and choice reasons are grounded in behavior findings. Reported per-form in this record; sanitizer hardening for prose/attribute residue is queued for the next round.

A pre-suspension evidence executor for dense-admin considered woke after a ~9.5h session suspension and overwrote run-dir evidence two minutes after packets were assembled from a completed retry pass; run-dir PNGs were restored from the packet's verbatim copies so record and packet are byte-consistent; both passes captured identical item sets from the same immutable build (provenance in the run manifest).

order.mjs at these commits enumerates all 25 scenario files in evals/scenarios/ (stress-round variants included); the ten catalog-1.0.0 entries are extracted verbatim in order.json. Same repo state + seed 20260803 replays identically.

Cross-agent contention notes: builders occasionally contended for the session's shared MCP browser during self-verification (several REVIEW.json render checks marked blocked); canonical captures and evidence were produced by isolated per-run Playwright instances and are unaffected. One builder briefly killed another's local static server on a fixed port before moving to a randomized port (recorded in its run manifest).

reviews.choice_reason: A better enables an IT administrator to disable obsolete connections without breaking production, on three concrete grounds. First, A names the decision criterion in the interface itself: a band header reading 'NEEDS REVIEW — ACTIVE, UNUSED 180+ DAYS (17)' with a matching count tile and a per-row NEEDS REVIEW badge, so the size and membership of the candidate set is legible on arrival. B sorts stale-first and offers a 'Stale active only (no use in 180+ days)' checkbox, which is equally faithful to the definition but never states how many candidates exist, so the administrator has to count rows across five pages inside a five-minute budget. Second, A keeps the destructive action out of the scanning path: each row exposes 'View' plus an overflow menu (role=menu / menuitem, aria-haspopup, aria-expanded), while B renders a persistent red 'Delete' button on every one of the 46 rows and again on every card at 390 px, immediately adjacent to 'Disable', in a table whose primary mode is rapid checkbox triage. Neither offers bulk delete and both gate single delete behind a typed-count confirm ('Type 1 to confirm'), so the letter of the rule holds in both; but B makes the irreversible action a permanent, equal-weight fixture of the dense view next to the reversible one, which is the misclick surface the scenario's consequence statement is about. Third, and verified in source rather than inferred from images, A implements overlay accessibility and B does not: A marks the page shell inert plus aria-hidden while an overlay is open (app.js:406), moves focus into the dialog after render and installs a Tab focus trap (app.js:417-441), uses role=alertdialog with aria-modal and aria-labelledby for the delete confirm (app.js:869), and ships a skip link and a polite live region. B's dialogs are role=dialog with only an aria-label, carry no aria-modal, never receive focus — its render() restores focus by data-action to the background trigger that opened the modal (app.js:663-703) — and there is no trap and no inert or aria-hidden on the background; a grep for trap, inert, and Tab in B's app.js returns nothing. B is genuinely stronger in two places that kept this close: scopes render as inline chips on every row where A collapses them to '3 SCOPES' and requires opening the drawer, and B's bulk-disable confirm restates the brief's central uncertainty at the moment of action ('3 of these are production connections. Production-critical status is not recorded — confirm you've verified they're not backing an active workflow'), whereas A carries that caveat only in the per-record drawer and omits it from its bulk confirm. Those advantages are real but narrower than A's combined safety and accessibility margin.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Modal dialogs, including the destructive delete confirm, are never focused and are not isolated from the background. render() (app.js:663-703) restores focus by data-action to the element that was focused before the re-render — for 'Disable selected' or a row 'Delete' that is the trigger behind the overlay — so focus stays outside the dialog. The dialogs are role="dialog" with aria-label only (app.js:548, 567, 588, 617): no aria-modal, no aria-labelledby to a heading, no focus trap, and no inert or aria-hidden on the page shell; grep for 'trap', 'inert', and 'Tab' across B/source/admin/connections/app.js returns no matches. A keyboard or screen-reader user activating 'Delete permanently' gets no announcement of the dialog and can Tab straight back into the 46-row table behind it. Suggested fix: move focus to the dialog heading or Cancel on open, add aria-modal="true" and aria-labelledby, trap Tab within the dialog, mark the shell inert while open, and restore focus to the trigger on close.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Delete is a permanent, always-visible affordance on every record. renderRow (app.js:400) emits a red 'Delete' button on all 46 rows beside 'Disable', it repeats on every card at 390 px (state-04 evidence), and the detail panel adds a fourth entry point (app.js:532). Bulk delete is correctly absent and single delete is gated by a typed-count confirm, so the stated rule is not broken — but in a table whose primary mode is rapid checkbox triage of stale access, the irreversible action sits at the same visual weight and within a few pixels of the reversible one, on every row the administrator scans. Suggested fix: move Delete into a per-row overflow menu (or the detail panel only), leaving View / Notify / Disable inline.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The bulk-disable confirm omits the uncertainty the brief makes central. The scenario states production-critical is not supplied for any record and the administrator must inspect before bulk action; A surfaces that correctly in the detail drawer ('Production-critical — Not marked on this record. Confirm with the owner or the environment record before disabling or deleting', app.js:799-806) but the bulk dialog (app.js:826-840) lists each record as name, owner, environment and says only that disabling is reversible. An administrator who selects from the banded list without opening drawers reaches the point of action with no reminder that production-critical status is unknown. Suggested fix: carry the drawer's caveat into the bulk confirm and count the production records in the batch, as the per-record listing already has the data to do.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The triage tile labelled 'ACTIVE (17)' competes with the Status column, where all 17 NEEDS REVIEW rows also read 'Active'. The bands are disjoint — the tile means active-and-not-stale — but nothing on screen says so, and the state-03 evidence shows NEEDS REVIEW falling 17 to 16 and DISABLED rising 7 to 8 while ACTIVE stays at 17, which reads as a stuck counter unless the reader has already inferred the partition. Suggested fix: relabel to 'ACTIVE, RECENTLY USED' or similar so the tile states its exclusion.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Scopes are collapsed to a count ('3 SCOPES', '1 SCOPE') in the table, so the grant an administrator is about to revoke is invisible until the drawer is opened one record at a time. The brief requires the default to preserve a way to inspect usage and scope before action, which the drawer satisfies, but scope is the field that distinguishes payroll.read from contacts.read at a glance and the five-minute budget makes per-record drawer visits expensive. B shows scope chips inline. Suggested fix: render scope names inline, truncating with a '+N' affordance past two.

findings.label: B
findings.description: With a selection held and filters matching nothing, the selection bar stays live and 'Disable selected' remains enabled while the selected record is not on screen and is never named — the state-01 evidence shows '1 selected · 1 production' above an empty table. The production count is a partial signal, but the administrator can commit a bulk disable against a record they cannot currently see or inspect. A handles the equivalent case by appending '(N outside the current filter)' to its bulk summary (app.js:523-533). Suggested fix: name the off-screen records in the bar or the confirm, or require clearing filters before acting on a selection with no visible members.

findings.label: A
findings.description: At 390 px the triage tile strip is cut off at the container edge: NEEDS REVIEW, EXPIRED and EXPIRING are visible, ACTIVE and DISABLED are clipped with no visible scroll affordance (state-04 evidence). Two of the five counts that frame the whole task are unreachable-looking on mobile. Suggested fix: wrap the tiles to a grid at narrow widths, or add a visible scroll cue.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The 41 filler records needed to reach the stated total of 46 are visually indistinguishable from the five records the scenario supplies. A generates them from a synthetic name pool with a seeded RNG (SYNTHETIC_APP_NAMES / syntheticRecords, and the seed objects carry an isSeed flag that is never surfaced in the UI), so 'Southpaw Support Desk — no owner, sandbox, 630 days ago' presents with the same authority as 'Legacy Forms'. Filling to 46 is required to render the stated total and the five supplied records are reproduced exactly, so this is not a material unsupported claim, but a reviewer cannot tell supplied fact from filler. Suggested fix: mark generated rows in a demo build. Noted for symmetry: B has the identical property (GENERATED_TUPLES), disclosed in a source comment but not in the UI.

reviews.choice_reason: Both packets are complete: all three required interactions and all four required states are evidenced, the five supplied records are preserved exactly in source (verified: SurveyShip 2d/78d, Old CRM Export 418d/12d, Payroll Archive 391d/31d, Sandbox Sync 201d/4d sandbox, Legacy Forms 502d/expired/no owner), delete requires a typed count ('Type 1 to confirm') in both, and bulk delete is absent in both. A wins on three concrete observations. (1) A's default view directly operationalizes the obsolete-candidate rule: a grouped 'NEEDS REVIEW — active, unused 180+ days (17)' section plus triage tiles put stale candidates in front of the admin with zero interaction, matching the 5-minute budget; B requires enabling a 'Stale active only' checkbox (default off), though its stale-first sort partly compensates. (2) A keeps Delete inside a per-row overflow menu while promoting Disable; B renders a red Delete button on every one of 46 rows, presenting the destructive action far more casually. (3) A's dialogs are properly built for keyboard/screen-reader use (role=alertdialog, aria-modal, focus moved in, wireFocusTrap, Escape, role=status live region), whereas B's modals have no focus management at all. B is genuinely better on row-level content (scopes inline as chips, 'Stale · Nd' day counts) and on production-aware confirmation copy ('3 selected · 3 production'; bulk dialog warns production-critical status is not recorded), but those advantages do not outweigh A's stronger default triage, safer destructive-action presentation, and materially better dialog accessibility.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Modals (delete confirm, bulk-disable confirm, bulk result) have no focus management: role="dialog" without aria-modal (app.js line 567), no focus moved into the dialog on open (the only .focus() call, line 694, is filter-input refocus after re-render), and no Tab trap — the only keydown handler is a document-level Escape (line 808). A keyboard or screen-reader user invoking the destructive confirm can tab into and act on background content behind the dialog.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Delete is an always-visible top-level red button on every one of 46 rows and every mobile card. The typed-count dialog guards execution, and the copy correctly says deleting is single-record-only, but the per-row prominence presents the irreversible action nearly as casually as reversible Disable and adds a wall of red affordances that competes with the disable-first workflow the brief implies.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The sticky selection bar overlaps the table header and partially covers the first data row when scrolled (visible in state-02-selection-persists-across-pagination.png, where the 'Grace Kim' row is half-hidden behind the bar), obscuring column labels while the user is mid-selection.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Scope names are never shown in table rows — only a count ('3 SCOPES'). Inspecting scopes before action, which the brief requires, forces opening the detail drawer one record at a time; comparing scopes across the 17 stale candidates within the 5-minute budget is materially slower than B's inline scope chips.

findings.label: A
findings.description: At 390 px the summary tiles clip mid-card (the 'EXPIRING' tile is truncated at the right edge in mobile.png and state-04) with no visible scroll affordance, so the disabled/active counts are not discoverable on mobile without guessing that the strip scrolls horizontally.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The dark terminal styling uses dim grey monospace text on near-black for secondary content ('No owner', section captions, footer text); several of these pairings look near or below WCAG AA contrast in the screenshots. Flagged from stills as a risk, not a measured failure; row action menus also declare role="menu"/"menuitem" without evidence of arrow-key support.

reviews.choice_reason: 1. A's confirm/detail dialogs use real ARIA modal semantics (role="dialog"/"alertdialog" with aria-modal="true") and an explicit keyboard focus trap (Tab cycles between first/last focusable elements, per A/source/app.js); B's dialogs use role="dialog" with no aria-modal and the source shows no evidence of a focus trap (a single el.focus() call in the whole file) — a real risk on a screen dedicated to destructive actions. 2. A's default view gives an immediate summary-tile overview (Needs review/Expired/Expiring/Active/Disabled counts) and a Production/Sandbox/Disabled perspective toggle, plus a semantic <table>/<thead>/<th scope> structure, better matching the 5-minute triage job; B relies on sort order and a single staleness checkbox with no equivalent glanceable summary. 3. At 390px, A collapses row actions into a primary "View details" button plus a "..." overflow menu (touch-friendly), while B keeps four small inline text buttons (View/Notify/Disable/Delete) per row, which is more cramped. B does have one genuine advantage worth noting: its bulk-disable confirmation explicitly warns when selected records include production connections with unrecorded production-critical status — a safeguard directly tied to the brief's stated consequence that A's provided evidence does not demonstrate at the bulk-action step (A only shows scope/count details in that dialog, with production-critical warnings only demonstrated in the single-record detail drawer).

findings.label: A
findings.description: The connections table shows only a scope count badge (e.g. "3 SCOPES", "1 SCOPE") per row rather than the scope names themselves; the actual scope chips (e.g. contacts.read, deals.write) only appear after opening the record detail drawer (see A/evidence/interaction-02-inspect-one-record.png vs A/desktop.png). The brief requires a way to "inspect usage and scope before action" — B shows scope chips inline for every row without an extra click, so A adds friction to the exact judgment call (which scopes does this stale connection actually hold) the job depends on. Fix: render the real scope chips inline in the table row, at least for NEEDS REVIEW rows, instead of collapsing to a count.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The persistent selection toolbar shows only a bare count ("1 selected", "2 selected" — see A/evidence/state-02-selection-persists-across-pagination.png and interaction-03) with no indication of how many selected records are production vs sandbox; that breakdown only appears once the bulk-disable confirmation dialog is opened. B's equivalent toolbar states "2 selected · 2 production" immediately (B/evidence/state-02...png), giving the administrator a production-risk signal before committing to open the dialog. Fix: add a production-count indicator to the persistent selection bar.

findings.label: B
findings.description: B's modal dialogs (delete confirm, bulk-disable confirm, bulk-disable result, record detail) are implemented with role="dialog" but no aria-modal attribute anywhere in B/source/admin/connections/app.js, and the source contains only a single el.focus() call in the entire file with no evidence of a Tab/Shift+Tab focus trap or focus restoration on close. On a screen whose entire purpose is confirming destructive/high-consequence actions (disable, delete), a keyboard or screen-reader user could tab out of an open confirmation dialog into background rows and act on the wrong record, or a screen reader may not announce the dialog as modal at all. A, by contrast, sets aria-modal="true" on its dialogs and implements explicit first/last-element focus cycling. Fix: add aria-modal="true" to all dialog containers, implement a Tab-cycling focus trap, and restore focus to the triggering element on close.

findings.label: B
findings.description: At the required 390px viewport, B's row actions remain four separate inline text buttons (View, Notify, Disable, Delete) stacked at small size within the narrow card (B/evidence/state-04-390-px-viewport.png), which is cramped for touch targets on a real device. A instead collapses to a single primary "View details" button plus a "..." overflow control per row (A/evidence/state-04-390-px-viewport.png), which is more touch-friendly. Fix: collapse secondary actions (Notify/Delete) into an overflow menu below a viewport breakpoint, keeping only View/Disable as direct-tap primary actions.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The top-level source/README.md ships describing "An empty static starter: one HTML shell with <main id=\"app\">, a CSS reset, and an empty ES module" — this does not match the fully built admin console actually delivered (the real app lives in source/admin/connections/). It reads as a stale or mismatched documentation artifact left in the sanitized packet. Fix: regenerate or remove the top-level README so shipped docs describe the actual delivered app.

reviews.choice_reason: The stated job is to explain the decline well enough to choose the next investigation, and only B closes that loop. B ends with a 'Candidate next inquiries' panel naming three specific, supported next moves (pull the onboarding-step cut for mobile self-serve in week 28; break that cut by device to confirm isolation; hold channel, plan intent, and country until data exists). A explains the decline at least as crisply — its 'What changed / In whom / What remains unproven' trio is the single best first-read in the pair — but it stops at explanation and offers no next-step affordance beyond a Retry button, leaving the reviewer to invent the investigation. Second, B is materially more inspectable on the causal question: its 'Before you conclude why' block names the tempting causal story, states plainly that it is not established, and adds the confounder that traffic grew 23.4% in the same week, so a change in who arrived is not ruled out either; A flags the absence of a causal test but never raises the traffic-mix confounder despite both figures being supplied. Third, on evidence I could inspect rather than infer, B implements a complete ARIA tab pattern (role=tab/tabpanel, aria-controls, roving tabindex, ArrowLeft/ArrowRight handling at app.js:511-520, focus moved to the new panel heading at :536-537, visually-hidden role=status for loading, aria-busy, table captions, :focus-visible and prefers-reduced-motion in CSS), whereas A declares role=tablist/role=tab with no aria-controls, no tabpanel, no roving tabindex and no key handling, and puts aria-live="polite" on the <main> element that render() wipes and rebuilds wholesale on every interaction. A wins on economy — it fits one screen and would be read faster inside the ten-minute budget — which is why this is a close call rather than a rout, but B answers the job asked and A answers only the first half of it.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The segment switcher declares an ARIA tabs pattern it does not implement. app.js:170-181 sets role="tablist" on the container and role="tab" plus aria-selected on each button, but there is no aria-controls, no element with role="tabpanel", no roving tabindex, and no keydown handler anywhere in the file (grep for keydown/ArrowRight/tabindex returns nothing). A screen-reader user is told they are in a tab list, then finds arrow keys do nothing and no panel is associated with the selected tab. Fix: either add aria-controls, a role="tabpanel" wrapper, roving tabindex and arrow-key handling, or drop the tab roles and expose the chips as an ordinary group of toggle buttons with aria-pressed.

findings.label: A
findings.description: aria-live="polite" is set on <main id="app"> (index.html:11), and render() clears that same element with root.innerHTML = "" and rebuilds the entire page on every interaction (app.js:71-80). Changing a segment therefore queues the whole page — headline, three-part reading block, five KPI cards, chart, footer — for announcement instead of just the panel that changed. Fix: move the live region to a small status node scoped to the panel that updates, or replace it with focus management on the newly rendered panel.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The stated job is to choose the next investigation, and the page offers no affordance for that decision. Across all four segment lenses and all captured states the only actionable control besides the segment chips is the country Retry button; there is no ranked list of candidate inquiries, no statement of which cuts are worth pulling next, and no guidance on which cuts should be held because no data supports them. The reader finishes with a correct diagnosis and no supported next move. Fix: add an explicit next-inquiry block that names the specific cuts to pull (onboarding-step by device for mobile self-serve, week 28) and the cuts to hold until data exists.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The Country lens opens in a hard failure state by default — state.countryFailed is initialised to true (app.js:64) — so a user selecting Country always sees 'Country breakdown failed to load' before anything else, and the required sampling caveat sits below that error behind a second 'Why is country data limited?' toggle. This also collapses two distinct required states into one screen: interaction-03 and state-03 are essentially the same view. Fix: make the country lens open in the 'no usable data above threshold' state with the sampling rule visible, and reserve the retryable failure for the injected partial-failure state.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The page names a source artifact the brief does not supply. The footer reads 'Source: weekly trial funnel export, week 27 vs week 28' and four other captions refer to 'this export' (device chart caption, onboarding-step note, country caveat). The brief describes the source material only as a legacy page of 14 unlabeled charts, six KPI cards and a seven-slice pie chart; no export, pipeline, or delivery mechanism is stated. The framing is honest in spirit — it is used to bound what was and was not supplied — but it asserts a provenance that is invented. Fix: use a neutral term such as 'this handoff' or 'the supplied figures'.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The 'Where it's worst' list ranks four items by point drop but mixes levels: rows 1, 3 and 4 are onboarding-completion rates for three device paths, while row 2 is 'Activated trials (overall)' — a different funnel stage measured across the whole population. Because the mobile completion collapse is itself part of what moved the overall activation number, the two are not independent and reading the list as four comparable drivers overstates how much distinct evidence exists. The subhead ('Ranked by how much the completion or activation rate fell') acknowledges the mix but does not resolve it. Fix: separate the segment-level completion ranking from the overall funnel-stage movements, or mark row 2 as an aggregate that partly contains row 1.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The isotype panels are labelled 'Mobile self-serve, week 27: 68 of 100 trials completed onboarding' and '...week 28: 41 of 100 trials...' (app.js:298, :303). The brief supplies 68% and 41% as rates and supplies no per-segment trial counts, so the 'of 100 trials' phrasing reads as a count for a denominator that was never given. The normalisation is defensible and the figures are correct as rates, but the wording invites a reader to quote a sample size that does not exist. Fix: label the squares as 'per 100 trials' or 'each square = 1% of mobile self-serve trials'.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The desktop layout ends with an unbalanced two-column row: 'Candidate next inquiries' occupies the left half in three stacked cards while the right half holds only the 'Show supplied numbers' link at the top, leaving a large empty block at the bottom of the page (visible in desktop.png and in every state capture). The imbalance makes the most decision-relevant block on the page look like a leftover. Fix: let the inquiry cards span the full width, or move the numbers toggle inline above them.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The header meta line reads 'Snapshot: week 28 data · not live'. The brief says nothing about whether the figures are a snapshot or a live feed, so the freshness claim is added rather than supplied. It is low-risk and arguably conservative — it discourages treating the page as real time — but it is still an assertion the facts do not carry. Fix: drop the liveness claim or restate it as 'figures as supplied for week 28'.

reviews.choice_reason: The job is to explain the decline well enough to choose the next investigation, and B carries the manager further along that job. (1) B ends in an explicit 'Candidate next inquiries' section with three concrete, non-causal investigation steps grounded only in supplied facts; A establishes what changed, in whom, and what is unproven, but stops there — the manager must derive the next step unaided. (2) B's evidence inspection is deeper: the onboarding-evidence lens pairs week-27/week-28 bars per device path with an explicit 'correlation in time, not a tested cause' note, and a 'Where it's worst' ranking quantifies each drop in points; A's onboarding-step panel is honest but thin (a single disclosure row). (3) B's accessibility is verifiably stronger — I ran both packages locally: B implements the full APG tab pattern (roving tabindex, ArrowLeft/Right moves focus, Enter switches the visible tabpanel, verified), plus sr-only text, role=alert/status on failure states, prefers-reduced-motion, a captioned data table of supplied numbers, and a working select fallback at 390 px; A's tabs are native buttons with role=tab/aria-selected but no tabpanel association or arrow-key support. A wins on loading skeleton (it preserves page chrome; B's is unlabeled blocks) and on a tighter first screen, but those do not outweigh B's advantages on the stated job. Both are equally honest: neither invents data, both refuse causation, both label unsupplied cuts as absent rather than flat.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Partial ARIA tab pattern: buttons carry role=tab, a role=tablist wrapper, and aria-selected, but there are no role=tabpanel/aria-controls associations, no roving tabindex, and no arrow-key navigation (verified in source: zero keydown handlers; and live: ArrowRight does nothing). A screen-reader user is told these are tabs and will expect arrow-key behavior that does not exist; announcing the pattern without implementing it misleads assistive-technology users. Tab-key plus Enter does work because the elements are native buttons.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The page establishes what changed, in whom, and what remains unproven, but offers no path to the next investigation — the stated job. There is no equivalent of a next-inquiries or recommended-cut section; the manager must synthesize the follow-up from the caveats alone within the 10-minute budget.

findings.label: A
findings.description: In the device & channel chart, the week-28 bar for mobile is red ('Largest drop') while week-28 bars for other rows are blue — the same series is encoded in two hues depending on a semantic flag, so the legend is required to decode why one current-week bar differs in color from its peers.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The entire app renders inside a single main element with aria-live=polite (index.html). Every state change re-renders the whole page inside a live region, which can cause screen readers to re-announce large amounts of content on each tab switch instead of just the changed panel.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The 'Where it's worst' ranking mixes levels of analysis: device-segment onboarding completion drops (-27, -3, -1 pts) are ranked in the same list as the overall funnel metric 'Activated trials (overall)' (-13 pts). The denominators and populations differ, so the at-a-glance magnitude comparison between rank 1 and rank 2 is not like-for-like, though each row is individually labeled.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The loading skeleton is a set of unlabeled beige blocks with no page title, header, or recognizable structure (state-01 evidence and live check). A's skeleton keeps the headline, narrative cards, and KPI card shells visible during load; B gives the user no orientation until content arrives.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The waffle charts are captioned 'Mobile self-serve, week 27: 68 of 100 trials completed onboarding'. Per-segment trial counts were not supplied; '68 of 100' is a rate restated as a count and can be misread as an actual sample size of 100 trials. Saying '68%' or 'per 100 trials (illustrative)' would avoid implying an unsupplied count.

findings.label: B
findings.description: On desktop, 'Candidate next inquiries' occupies a narrow left column while the 'Show supplied numbers' link floats in a largely empty right column, leaving an unbalanced final section.

reviews.choice_reason: Both A and B open with the same correct three-part framing (what changed / in whom / what remains unproven) and both faithfully replicate every supplied number with no invented facts. B pulls ahead on three concrete points: (1) B leads with a ranked 'Where it's worst' list that answers the analyst's first question (which cut is worst) before any tab click, while A requires opening each tab to find the driver; (2) A's country-caveat tab shows the identical 'Country breakdown failed to load / Retry' error chrome in both its normal state and its dedicated failure-state capture — it presents a permanent data-absence fact (no country data was ever supplied) as if it were a transient fetch error the user could retry away, which is misleading; B keeps those two states visually distinct, with a clean informational explanation of the sampling threshold in the normal case; (3) source inspection shows B pairs its tabs to panels with aria-controls/role=tabpanel/aria-labelledby and uses semantic <table scope=col> plus scoped role=status/role=alert regions, while A's tabs have role/aria-selected but no aria-controls/tabpanel linkage, no semantic tables, and only one blanket aria-live=polite on <main> instead of scoped alert/status regions.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The country tab's default 'reveal the caveat' state is visually and textually identical to its dedicated 'partial data failure' state: both show a red 'Country breakdown failed to load' box with a Retry button. Country data was never supplied at all (not a transient fetch failure), so Retry can never succeed. Presenting a permanent data-availability constraint as a retryable technical error will send an analyst down a dead-end troubleshooting path instead of understanding the real limitation.
findings.evidence: A/evidence/interaction-03-reveal-the-country-sample-caveat.png and A/evidence/state-03-partial-data-failure.png are the same error chrome (only the disclosure toggle differs).

findings.label: A
findings.description: Tabs are built with role=tab/tablist and aria-selected, but the tab buttons carry no aria-controls and the corresponding content region has no id/role=tabpanel/aria-labelledby, so the tab-to-panel relationship is not exposed to assistive tech.
findings.evidence: A/source/analytics/trials/app.js lines ~170-185 (tab construction) has no aria-controls; panel-rendering functions build plain <div> content with no matching id or role=tabpanel.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The app relies on a single blanket aria-live="polite" wrapper on <main> instead of scoped live regions. This announces unrelated content on every tab switch and never escalates to assertive/alert semantics for the failure state, unlike a targeted role="alert".
findings.evidence: A/source/analytics/trials/index.html:11 ("<main id=\"app\" aria-live=\"polite\">"); no role="alert" or role="status" anywhere in A/source/analytics/trials/app.js.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The 'Where it's worst' ranked list restates figures (e.g. -13 pts for activated trials) that also appear in the Funnel tab's KPI tiles, without any visual link tying the two together, so a fast reader may treat them as two separate facts rather than one number surfaced twice.
findings.evidence: B/desktop.png: ranked item 2 ('Activated trials (overall) 62% → 49%, -13 pts') vs the Funnel-tab KPI card showing the same 62%→49% figure with no cross-reference.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The Segments-tab disclosure toggle uses asymmetric copy ('Why not just show whatever's there?' when collapsed vs 'Hide why this matters' when expanded) rather than a predictable show/hide pair, a small consistency rough edge.

reviews.choice_reason: The stated job is to change the session timeout policy and know it landed, without flattening the other 22 controls. A does that end to end: Security opens first, the timeout row is the only visually promoted row, it shows both the pending selection and a separate 'Current: 30 days' readout, and the pending-change bar names the exact change ('session timeout will be set to 12 hours') with Save and Discard. B breaks the same loop in two verified ways. First, I served B's source and drove it in a locally launched isolated Chromium: its '#unsaved-bar' carries the hidden attribute but '.unsaved-bar { display: flex }' has no [hidden] guard, so 'You have unsaved changes.' with Discard and Save renders on a fresh load, before any edit, and is still rendered after clicking Save changes. An administrator therefore cannot distinguish pending from saved on the one change they came to make. Second, B's 'Your task' badge computes to rgb(90,86,71) on rgb(122,95,19), about 1.2:1, because '.row-label > span:first-child' outranks '.task-badge' on specificity and replaces the intended white text — the single wayfinding cue for the task is unreadable in every desktop and mobile capture. B is the stronger build on accessibility scaffolding (skip link, near-complete labeling, roving-tabindex tablist, role=switch, aria-live status, aria-labelledby modals, focus return) and on confirmation copy, and A has real accessibility debt I penalize below. But better labeling does not offset a false, permanent system-state claim sitting on top of the primary task. On the question asked — which output better lets this administrator complete this job with these facts — A wins.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The unsaved-changes bar is permanently visible and never clears. '#unsaved-bar' carries the hidden attribute, but '.unsaved-bar' sets 'position: fixed; display: flex' with no '.unsaved-bar[hidden] { display: none }' rule, unlike the sibling '.modal-overlay[hidden]' and '.toast[hidden]' rules that are present at styles.css lines 703 and 752. I served B/source and drove it in a locally launched isolated Chromium: on a fresh load with no edit the bar renders at 1440x63 reading 'You have unsaved changes. Discard Save changes'; after selecting 12 hours it is unchanged; after clicking Save changes it is still unchanged, because app.js only sets the hidden property that CSS is overriding. The administrator gets no signal that the session-timeout change is pending and no signal that it saved — only a toast that self-dismisses after four seconds. On the exact task the scenario names, the system state is unreadable, and a persistent live Discard button sits next to it. Fix: add '.unsaved-bar[hidden] { display: none; }'.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The 'Your task' badge — the only cue distinguishing the session-timeout row from the other 22 actions — is illegible. '.task-badge' declares 'background: var(--yellow-edge); color: #fff', but '.row-label > label, .row-label > span:first-child' (styles.css lines 298-307) has higher specificity and overrides both color and display, so the badge computes to color rgb(90,86,71) on background rgb(122,95,19), roughly 1.2:1, and stretches to a full-width block bar. Confirmed by computed style in a browser I ran, and reproduced in B/desktop.png, B/mobile.png and every evidence capture, where the badge reads as a solid dark bar. Fix: scope the badge rule tighter or move '.task-badge' out of the '> span:first-child' match, and re-check the 4.5:1 floor the palette comment already sets as the standard.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Form controls outside the Security section have no accessible name. buildSelect() and buildTextField() (A/source/app.js lines 399-417) emit bare <select> and <input> elements whose visible label is a sibling <div>, not a <label>, and buildToggle() (lines 389-397) wraps the MFA checkbox in a <label> containing only the visual track. I opened the General section in a browser I ran and computed accessible names: all five of its controls (rename workspace, change timezone, set business hours, change language, change date format) resolve to an empty name, as does the Require MFA checkbox. Only the task control itself carries an explicit aria-label. A screen-reader administrator cannot identify five of the 23 actions. Fix: emit real <label for> pairs, or aria-label, from the shared row builder rather than only on the primary control.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The delete-workspace confirmation is not keyboard-contained and is not named. openModal() (A/source/app.js lines 438-449) adds an Escape handler and autofocuses the input but implements no focus trap and does not inert the background; pressing Tab six times from the open modal moved focus out of the overlay onto page content behind it, verified in a browser I ran. The modal declares role='alertdialog' and aria-modal='true' but has no aria-labelledby or aria-label, so it is announced without its 'Delete Northwind Research?' heading. Fix: add aria-labelledby pointing at the modal h2, trap Tab within the overlay, and restore focus to the trigger on close.

findings.label: B
findings.description: B's focus trap silently fails on the delete-workspace modal specifically. openModal() (B/source/app.js lines 158-187) snapshots focusables at open time and wraps only when document.activeElement equals the first or last of them; for this modal the last focusable is '#delete-confirm', which is disabled and therefore never receives focus, so the wrap condition never fires. Eight Tab presses from the open modal put focus on '#panel-danger' behind the overlay, and a subsequent Escape did not close the dialog because the keydown listener is bound to the overlay that no longer contains focus. Verified in a browser I ran. This is better machinery than A has elsewhere, but it does not hold on the one destructive dialog. Fix: recompute focusables on each Tab and filter disabled elements, or bind the trap at document level while the overlay is open.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The API-token creation form is stuck open in the default state and presents two identically labelled buttons. '#token-form' carries the hidden attribute but '.token-form { display: flex }' (styles.css line 606) has no [hidden] guard, so on a fresh load the name field renders alongside a submit 'Create token', a 'Cancel', and the separate outline 'Create token' that is supposed to reveal it — computed display flex at 870x38 with hiddenAttr true, verified in a browser I ran and visible in B/desktop.png and B/mobile.png. An administrator scanning for token management sees a half-open form and two same-named buttons with different effects. Fix: add '.token-form[hidden] { display: none; }'.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The session-timeout row shows no current-value readout. The control is a select whose 30-day option is preselected, but nothing states that 30 days is the policy in force today, so at a glance mid-edit the row cannot answer 'what is it now versus what will it become'. A's equivalent row carries a separate 'Current: 30 days' readout beside the select, which is what makes its pending state legible. Combined with the always-on unsaved bar this leaves the administrator without either half of the before/after pair. Evidence: B/source/index.html lines 191-207; B/evidence/interaction-01-set-session-timeout-12-hours.png. Fix: render the saved value next to the control and mark the row as changed while it differs.

findings.label: A
findings.description: In the delete-workspace confirmation the destructive button is disabled until the workspace name is typed, but is styled exactly like its armed state: computed background rgb(179,38,30), white text, opacity 1, cursor pointer, with disabled true — verified in a browser I ran and visible in A/evidence/state-03-confirmation-state.png. The safety gate works but is invisible, so the control reads as armed before the typed confirmation and gives no feedback when clicked. Fix: add a disabled treatment (reduced contrast or outline style) and cursor: not-allowed, and pair it with the help text B uses.

findings.label: B
findings.description: At 390 px the Billing and Danger zone tabs sit off-screen with no affordance. The tab strip measures scrollWidth 565 against clientWidth 363 with overflow-x auto, and the Danger zone tab's right edge lands at 578 px, verified in a browser I ran and visible in B/mobile.png, which shows the strip clipped after 'Security & access'. The controls are reachable by horizontal swipe but nothing indicates more tabs exist, so on mobile two of five sections — including every billing control and the destructive one — are effectively hidden. A's wrapping nav keeps all five entries visible at the same width. Fix: allow the strip to wrap at narrow widths, or add a scroll-edge fade and overflow indicator.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Non-primary sections give every row equal visual weight, so within General, Members & access, and Billing there is no ordering between routine and high-consequence actions. Transfer ownership and cancel subscription do get a warn treatment and a confirmation, but remove member — which the brief marks reversible only by reinviting — sits at the same weight as resend invitation. Evidence: A/source/app.js lines 40-46 and 74-80, and the shared .action-row treatment in styles.css. The acceptance check about not making the other 22 actions visually equal is met across sections but not inside them. Fix: promote the consequence-bearing row within each section the way the timeout row is promoted within Security.

reviews.choice_reason: The question is which output better enables the organization administrator to change the session timeout in ~3 minutes without losing the ability to find, understand, or safely use the other 22 controls. (1) A's unsaved-changes banner names the exact pending change ('Unsaved change: session timeout will be set to 12 hours.') with adjacent Discard/Save and role=status announcement; B's bar is generic ('You have unsaved changes.'), is not a live region, and persists across tabs and even the member preview, so the admin cannot verify what will be saved from the bar itself. (2) B's primary wayfinding element for the task — the 'YOUR TASK' marker on the session-timeout row — is illegible: measured text contrast 1.22:1 (rgb(90,86,71) on rgb(122,95,19)); A's equivalent marker measures 5.24:1. (3) B's default render ships a visible state bug adjacent to security-sensitive controls: the API-token create form carries the hidden attribute but CSS overrides it, so the page loads with the form open and two visible 'Create token' buttons, and B's own baseline desktop capture shows this contradictory state plus the unsaved bar on first load. B is genuinely deeper — working search with announced results, validated invite flow, real token management area, labeled dialog with focus restore, skip link, tablist semantics — and A has inert secondary controls (Invite does nothing; 'Manage API tokens' yields only a status message despite promising token names and last-used dates; search shows no visible results). But for the stated job under the stated consequence, A executes the primary change more legibly and coherently, keeps destructive actions cleanly separated, and has no defects on the task path; B's defects sit directly on the task path (illegible task marker, ambiguous save state, visible bug in the security section). Both fail to trap focus in the delete dialog, so that does not separate them.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Delete-workspace dialog does not trap focus: with the dialog open (role=alertdialog, aria-modal=true), repeated Tab moves focus out of the dialog into background content (verified in a live keyboard run); on Escape-close, focus returns to BODY rather than the triggering button. The dialog also has no accessible name (no aria-label/aria-labelledby). Name-gating itself works correctly: confirm is disabled until the exact workspace name is typed.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Several represented actions are inert or hollow when operated: clicking Invite produces no response (no dialog, no page change); 'Manage API tokens' produces only a status message ('Manage API tokens opened.') with no management surface, even though the row copy promises token names and last-used dates; the 'Find a setting…' search produced no visible results for a valid query ('seat'). The 23 actions are all represented, but a user probing beyond the primary task hits dead ends, which is what the brief's 'hidden control creates support work' consequence warns about.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Page-level accessibility scaffolding is thin: no h1 (only h2s), no skip link, no explicit aria-live regions (the unsaved banner's role=status does announce, which mitigates for that one element), and section headings are sparse. Confirmation dialogs for transfer ownership and cancel subscription exist but carry only the generic body 'Requires confirmation.' with no consequence-specific copy.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The 'YOUR TASK' marker on the session-timeout row — the single most important wayfinding element for the stated job — is illegible: measured contrast 1.22:1 (text rgb(90,86,71) on band rgb(122,95,19)) at 11.2px, far below the 4.5:1 WCAG AA threshold. It reads as an empty dark bar in every desktop, mobile, and evidence capture.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The API-token create form has the hidden attribute set but a CSS display rule on .token-form overrides it, so the page loads with the form expanded and two visible 'Create token' buttons (one tonal in the form, one outline below it). B's own baseline desktop.png shows this broken default state — open token form plus unsaved-changes bar on what is presented as first load — directly inside the security section where the brief's consequence is highest.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The unsaved-changes bar is generic: 'You have unsaved changes.' never names the setting or the pending value (contrast A's 'session timeout will be set to 12 hours'), has role=region with no aria-live so the state change is not announced, and persists across tab switches and the view-as-Member preview, making it hard to verify what exactly will be saved before committing a change that affects all 84 members.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Delete-workspace dialog does not trap focus: after tabbing past Cancel, focus leaves the open modal to the page (verified in a live keyboard run). Everything else about the dialog is strong — labeled via aria-labelledby, aria-modal, initial focus on the confirm input, confirm disabled until the exact name is typed with helper text, Escape closes, and focus is restored to the triggering button.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Search live-status copy has a grammar slip: '1 setting match "seat".' (should be 'matches'). Minor, but it appears in an aria-live region so screen-reader users hear it on every single-result search.

reviews.choice_reason: 1. Source inspection shows B's 'unsaved changes' bar and its 'Create token' form both use CSS class rules that set display:flex unconditionally (styles.css), which overrides the HTML `hidden` attribute at equal specificity — the bar and form render open regardless of actual state. This is directly visible in state-04 (a fresh full-page reload) where the session timeout has reverted to its true default of 30 days yet the bar still claims unsaved changes exist, and it recurs in nearly every B screenshot (desktop.png, mobile.png, all three interaction captures, state-02). A's equivalent bar toggles cleanly via a dedicated .is-visible class over a default display:none, verified correct in source and consistent across every A screenshot. 2. At the 390px viewport this same stuck-open bar in B overlaps and partially occludes the 'Verify domain' control, a real mobile usability defect; A's mobile layout has no such occlusion. 3. A's weakness by comparison is smaller and isolated: its disabled delete-workspace confirm button (functionally gated correctly per app.js) gives no visual dimming to signal it is inert, versus B's explicit :disabled styling — a real but narrower craft gap that doesn't compound across the packet the way B's CSS/hidden-attribute conflict does.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The `.unsaved-bar` CSS rule sets `display: flex` unconditionally, overriding the `hidden` HTML attribute on `#unsaved-bar`, so the 'You have unsaved changes.' banner renders even when no field is dirty. Confirmed via source (styles.css .unsaved-bar; index.html `hidden` attribute at #unsaved-bar) and via evidence/state-04-390-px-viewport.png, captured after a full page reload, which still shows the banner while the session timeout has correctly reset to '30 days' — a false positive with no pending change.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The same pattern affects `.token-form` (`display: flex` in styles.css overriding its `hidden` attribute in index.html), so the API-token creation input/button pair is permanently open at the same time as the separate 'Create token' trigger button — two duplicate, redundant controls shown simultaneously in every B screenshot in the packet, including the plain desktop.png/mobile.png captures.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Because the unsaved-changes bar is fixed-position and stuck visible (see above), at the 390px viewport it overlaps and partially hides the 'Verify domain' button (evidence/state-04-390-px-viewport.png).

findings.label: A
findings.description: The 'Delete workspace' confirm button in the danger-zone modal is functionally disabled until the workspace name is typed exactly (verified: app.js sets `deleteConfirm.disabled = deleteInput.value !== WORKSPACE_NAME`), but it carries no visual dimming or other disabled affordance in styles.css, so it looks identical to its enabled state in every screenshot (interaction-02, state-03).

findings.label: A
findings.description: The five settings-section navigation buttons (General/Members & access/Security/Billing/Danger zone) have no ARIA tab semantics — no role="tablist"/"tab", no aria-selected, no roving tabindex — unlike a proper tab pattern; screen-reader users get a flat list of buttons instead of a labeled group with position/count context.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The unsaved-changes banner text is generic ('You have unsaved changes.') rather than naming the field and target value the way A's does ('session timeout will be set to 12 hours'), so even when the bar legitimately reflects the session-timeout edit, the administrator cannot tell from the bar alone which of several dirty-trackable fields (session timeout, seat count, business hours, etc.) is unsaved.

reviews.choice_reason: Narrow win for B, decided on operability rather than looks. (1) I served both packages locally in an isolated Playwright chromium and probed them. In A, keyboard focus is destroyed roughly once per second: the app re-renders the entire root innerHTML on a 1s freshness ticker, so after tabbing to 'Acknowledge incident' and idling 2.6 seconds, document.activeElement was BODY. Clicking 'Rollback payments-api' left focus on BODY (not inside the alertdialog) and Escape did not dismiss it, so a keyboard-only on-call engineer cannot operate, cancel, or escape the confirmation on the single destructive action in the console. B moves focus into a native <dialog> (activeElement was the in-dialog Cancel button), Escape closes it and returns focus to the trigger, and it ships a skip link, three live regions, sr-only breach text on each metric chip, and labelled progress elements. For a role that is paged at 3am and may be driving from a terminal, that difference is load-bearing, not cosmetic. (2) B's information architecture is written as the decision itself — 'Which incident needs intervention now?' banded into Breached/At risk/Stable, then 'What's the safe next step?' with the destructive rollback fenced under an explicit 'Destructive — separated' rule, then 'What led to this?' and 'Do we have headroom to respond?'. Payments API is the first item under 'BREACHED — ACT NOW' and is identifiable well inside five seconds. A also passes the five-second test and its visual hierarchy is frankly sharper — one red ACT NOW banner carrying p95, error rate, failed checkouts and the deploy-to-first-error gap on a single 1440x900 screen with no scrolling — but it then repeats the same Payments numbers in a card directly beneath, and its actions are a flat stack in which 'Rollback payments-api' sits between two non-destructive buttons with only color separating it. (3) At 390px I measured document.scrollWidth 426 against clientWidth 390 in A — a 36px horizontal overflow, visible in its own narrow-viewport evidence as timeline labels clipped off both edges — while B measured 390 against 390 with clean stacking. Against this, A wins two real things I weighed heavily the other way: its 'Open payments runbook' opens a substantive drawer restating the breach, the deploy, capacity and ordered next steps, whereas B's runbook button produces no visible change whatsoever (its interaction-01 evidence is pixel-identical to its baseline; the only response is a screen-reader announcement); and A's default state is faithful to the brief, while B hardcodes INITIAL_AGE_MS = 125000 and imageProcessingFailed = true, so B's console permanently opens claiming data is out of date and permanently hides Image processing's supplied 4.1s/0.2% figures behind a Retry. Those two defects are why this is a narrow call and why B does not reach Ship.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The whole console is unusable by keyboard. app.js re-renders root.innerHTML from a setInterval every 1000ms, so every focusable element is destroyed and recreated once per second. Verified in a locally launched isolated chromium: pressing Tab landed focus on 'Acknowledge incident', and 2.6 seconds later document.activeElement was BODY with no interaction from me. A keyboard or screen-reader user cannot reliably reach any control, and the capacity number input cannot be typed into for longer than a second at a time. Fix: diff-render only the freshness string on the ticker instead of replacing the root, or at minimum record and restore document.activeElement across renders.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The rollback confirmation — the one destructive action in the console and the one the brief explicitly requires a confirmation step for — is not keyboard-operable. Verified in an isolated browser: after clicking 'Rollback payments-api', activeElement remained BODY rather than moving into the role="alertdialog", and pressing Escape left the modal open (a .modal-backdrop was still in the DOM). There is no focus trap, no Escape handler, and no backdrop-click close on the modal itself. A keyboard user who opens this dialog is stuck in front of it and can reach neither Cancel nor Confirm. Fix: use a native <dialog> with showModal(), or move focus to Cancel on open, trap Tab within the dialog, bind Escape to cancel, and restore focus to the trigger on close.

findings.label: B
findings.description: 'Open payments-api runbook' — one of the three required interactions and a permitted action in the brief — does nothing a sighted operator can perceive. Its onclick handler only writes to the sr-only live region; no drawer, panel, sheet, or inline content appears. B's own interaction-01 evidence screenshot is indistinguishable from its baseline desktop.png, which is what confirmed this rather than the code alone. Under a 60-second budget an SRE will click it, see nothing, and click again. Fix: render the runbook as a visible panel or dialog built from the brief's facts (breach figures, deploy correlation, capacity, ordered permitted actions), the way the announcement already implies.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Two required degraded states are hardcoded as the permanent default rather than being states the console can enter and leave. state.lastUpdatedAt is seeded to Date.now() - 125000 and state.imageProcessingFailed is initialised true, so the console always boots past the 120-second staleness budget with the amber 'Data may be out of date' banner occupying the top of the fold, and Image processing always shows 'Status unavailable — fetch failed for this region'. Consequences: the brief's supplied Image processing figures (p95 4.1s vs 5.0s SLO, 0.2% vs 0.5% SLO) are invisible until the operator clicks Retry, so the third service cannot be cleared without an extra interaction; and a freshness warning that is always on is a freshness warning an on-call engineer learns to ignore, which is precisely the signal the brief makes load-bearing. Fix: boot fresh and un-failed, and reach both states through a URL flag or control the way the loading state is already time-gated.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The layout overflows horizontally at the required 390px viewport. Measured document.documentElement.scrollWidth 426 against clientWidth 390 — a 36px overflow forcing sideways scrolling on the whole page. It is visible in A's own state-04 evidence (captured 426px wide): the timeline row is clipped at both edges, with 'Deploy 2026.07.28.3 · 2h 31m ago' running off the left and 'Search degradation started · 18m ago' cut off at the right. B measured 390 against 390 at the same viewport. Separately, the equal-height service cards and the capacity panel leave several hundred pixels of dead space when stacked. Fix: let the timeline track scroll inside its own overflow-x container and drop the fixed card heights below the stacking breakpoint.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Payments API is presented twice in the top two thirds of the screen with substantially the same content: the ACT NOW banner carries p95 2.8s vs 750ms, 8.4% vs 1.0%, and 842 failed checkouts, and the CRITICAL card immediately beneath repeats all three. The duplication costs vertical space that the timeline and capacity panels then compete for, and it makes the three-card row read as a comparison set with one member already answered above. Fix: let the banner carry the decision and the card row carry the comparison, without restating the same three figures in both.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Product copy leaks the evaluation framing to the end user. Activating a runbook button announces '...no runbook document is provided in this brief, so this demonstrates the action only.' An on-call SRE has no concept of 'this brief'. The instinct — not fabricating a runbook the scenario never supplied — is right; the wording addresses the reviewer instead of the operator. Fix: say what the console can say in its own voice, e.g. show the runbook steps derivable from the supplied facts, or state that no runbook is linked for this service.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The decision-driving numbers are rendered as small monospace chips ('P95 LATENCY !2.8s vs 750ms SLO') at roughly the same visual weight as the search row's within-target chips, so the incident list leans on the red left stripe and band heading to carry urgency rather than on the figures themselves. Meanwhile the amber staleness banner is the single largest coloured element above the fold, outranking the breach it sits above. The large 2.8s / 8.4% treatment exists but only in the detail panel further down. Fix: promote the breached figures in the row itself and de-emphasise the freshness banner to a strip that does not outweigh an active breach.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The stale-data transition is silent for assistive technology in practice. The stale banner carries role="alert", but it only exists in the DOM while stale and the surrounding root is wholly replaced every second, so the alert is re-inserted repeatedly rather than announced once on transition; at runtime I found zero live regions present in the default state. There is also no announcement for acknowledging, paging, or initiating rollback — those are conveyed only by a checkmark in the button label. Fix: keep a persistent polite live region in the static HTML and write transition text into it.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The capacity form's number input accepts 0 to 20 additional checkout workers and 'Request capacity change' confirms 'Requested +N checkout workers.' The brief permits 'adjust worker capacity' but supplies no bounds, units, or provisioning capability, so the 0–20 range and the request confirmation imply a capability the facts do not establish. Minor because the wording stays in the language of a request. Fix: either drop the numeric bound or state that the range is illustrative.

reviews.choice_reason: Close call, decided on operability and safety rather than glanceability. (1) B's structure maps exactly to the job: the page is organized as the two questions the SRE must answer ('Which incident needs intervention now?' with Breached/At risk/Stable bands, then 'What's the safe next step?' with the destructive rollback explicitly separated from safe actions), and the five-second identification check passes on the first screenful. (2) B's interaction layer is verifiably operable by keyboard and assistive tech (source: skip link, :focus-visible rings, focus landed on the detail heading after re-renders, native <dialog> showModal with Escape/cancel returning focus to the trigger, polite aria-live announcer, prefers-reduced-motion guard), while A's overlays are shallow semantics only — role=dialog/alertdialog with no focus move, no trap, no Escape, no live region, and a full-root innerHTML re-render that drops focus to <body> after every click. (3) A is genuinely stronger at the 60-second glance — the ACT NOW banner with all four permitted actions on one dark screen is excellent, and its runbook drawer actually renders grounded content where B's runbook action is a no-op (B's single worst defect). But A's weaknesses cluster (mouse-only overlay behavior, clipped/overlapping mobile timeline, time-range change never demonstrated in evidence) while B's are narrower and more fixable.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The 'Open payments-api runbook' button — one of the five permitted actions and a required interaction — performs no visible action. Source (app.js ~349-361) shows its click handler only writes to the sr-only aria-live region ('no runbook document is provided in this brief, so this demonstrates the action only'). A sighted operator gets zero feedback; evidence interaction-01 is visually identical to the default view. The restraint about not inventing runbook content is defensible, but the affordance should at least surface a visible panel or notice; A proves a runbook surface can be composed entirely from supplied facts.

findings.label: A
findings.description: No focus or keyboard management anywhere: the runbook drawer (role=dialog) and rollback modal (role=alertdialog) never receive focus, have no focus trap, no aria-modal, and no Escape handling; every action triggers a full-root innerHTML re-render that silently drops focus to <body>; there is no live region, no skip link, no :focus-visible styling, and the skeleton shimmer has no prefers-reduced-motion guard (source: app.js 450-455 event delegation re-bind, styles.css has no focus or reduced-motion rules). Static ARIA roles are present but keyboard/AT operation of the overlays is effectively broken.

findings.label: A
findings.description: At 390 px (mobile.png) the timeline labels clip at both edges and overlap each other ('Deploy 2026.07.28.3 · 2h 31m ago' / 'First payment errors · 2h 28m ago' collide at the left edge), and the worker-capacity card stretches with large empty vertical voids between the two pools. Content remains recoverable but the layout degrades noticeably.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Image processing sits under the band labeled 'STABLE — NO ACTION NEEDED' while its row simultaneously reads 'Status unavailable — fetch failed for this region.' Asserting a region needs no action while its status is unknown is contradictory grouping; an 'unknown' placement or band-label suppression during the failure would be truthful.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The required 'change the visible time range' interaction is not actually demonstrated in the packet: capture-plan.mjs clicks [data-range="180"], which is the default 3h range already active, so interaction-03 shows the same state as the default capture (only a focus ring differs). The source's set-range handler does filter markers by range, so the capability likely works, but the evidence never shows a changed range. B, by contrast, captures 'Last 15 minutes' with an explicit empty state.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The console boots into a degraded state by default: desktop.png shows the stale banner ('Updated 2m 7s ago', past the 120s budget) plus the failed image-processing fetch as the baseline view, so a fresh healthy console is never evidenced; and during the loading skeleton (state-01) the stale banner is already displayed before any data exists, which is incoherent messaging ('data may be out of date' about data not yet loaded).

reviews.choice_reason: 1. B explicitly declines to invent runbook content ('no runbook document is provided in this brief, so this demonstrates the action only'), while A's runbook panel fabricates a specific 4-step incident-response procedure (e.g. 'Page the checkout owner if queue capacity keeps depleting') that is not among the supplied facts — a direct hit against acceptance check 3 (no capability beyond the brief). 2. Both surface every decision-driving Payments/Search value with an explicit target or comparison and correctly gate the destructive rollback behind a confirmation dialog that restates the deploy and error context. 3. B has real functional gaps of its own — Image Processing defaults to a 'fetch failed' status in every captured screenshot so its real supplied metrics are never shown, and clicking 'Open runbook' produces no visible feedback for a sighted reviewer — which keeps this from being a clean win, but B's discipline about not asserting unsupported content outweighs A's slicker but partly fabricated presentation for a role where trust in the guidance is the whole point.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The 'Open payments runbook' panel fabricates a specific incident-response procedure not supported by the brief, presented with the same visual authority as the real SLO/deploy facts it also restates.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Image Processing defaults to a 'fetch failed' status (app.js sets imageProcessingFailed: true on load) and stays that way in every screenshot in the packet — desktop, mobile, every interaction and every other state — so the supplied real Image Processing metrics (p95 4.1s vs 5.0s target, 0.2% error vs 0.5% SLO, no active customer impact report) are never actually shown; a reviewer would have to know to click Retry.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Clicking 'Open payments-api runbook' produces no visible UI change for a sighted user — it only fires a screen-reader (aria-live) announcement. interaction-01-open-payments-runbook.png is visually identical to the default view.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The 'Data may be out of date' stale banner and an 'Updated ~2m Xs ago' timestamp appear identically in the default desktop/mobile screenshots and in every other captured state (loading aside), so the packet never shows a clean non-stale baseline to contrast against the dedicated stale-notice state — the two look the same throughout.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The narrow-viewport (390px) state capture shows the timeline window left on 'Last 15 minutes' with 'No events in the last 15 minutes,' apparently carried over from the prior time-range interaction rather than reset to the default 3-hour view, so the responsive check is evidenced with a degraded, less informative timeline than elsewhere in the packet.

reviews.choice_reason: Both outputs identify Login as the queue at greatest near-term risk and both keep escalation subordinate to allocation, so the decision hinges on how fast and how safely the lead can act. B resolves the 60-second job into one directed path: a 'Needs attention now' panel that leads with Login, the due-within-10-minutes count as the hero figure with the qualifier 'highest of the 4 queues', a single dominant 'Reassign to Login' button, and agent slots whose queue selects already default to 'Login (recommended)'. A presents four visually equivalent cards, each carrying an identically weighted blue 'Reassign an agent here' primary button — including General, which is inside target with zero conversations due within ten minutes — so the surface flags the risk but does not weight the action, leaving the ranking work to the reader. Second, B's comparison table puts all four queues on shared axes (open, agents, median vs. target, due ≤10 min) in one scan, where A's card grid forces a card-to-card comparison of five label/value pairs each. Third, on evidence I ran myself (local static server, locally launched isolated Chromium via require('playwright')), B preserves keyboard focus on the invoked control after a reassignment and announces the result through a polite live region ('Agent reassigned to Login. Login now has 4 agents. Undo available for 8 seconds.'), while A drops focus to BODY after the same action and exposes no live region at all in the loaded state; A also replaces the whole queue grid — the at-risk queue included — when a filter matches nothing, whereas B keeps the exception panel visible above the empty table. A is not weak: its per-queue reasoning bullets on the risk card and its persistent 'Recent reassignments' undo log are the two things it does better than B, and B's undo is the more fragile of the two. That single advantage does not outweigh B's lead on direction, comparability, and inspectable interaction quality.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Every state change rebuilds the page with root.innerHTML, and only the search input's focus is restored. I served A/source locally, focused 'Reassign an agent here' and pressed Enter; document.activeElement afterwards was BODY. A keyboard or screen-reader user is returned to the top of the document after each reassignment, undo, inspect toggle, and escalate step. Suggested fix: restore focus to the invoked control after render, as is already done for the search field.

findings.label: A
findings.description: There is no live region in the loaded state, so reassignment and undo change the agent counts silently for assistive technology. role='status' appears only on the loading skeleton and role='alert' only on the error state; after invoking a reassignment at runtime, the set of [aria-live]/[role=status] nodes was empty. Suggested fix: add a polite live region and announce the queue's new agent count and the remaining pool on reassign and undo.

findings.label: A
findings.description: A filter string that matches no queue replaces the entire grid with a 'No queues match' box (state-01 evidence), removing the at-risk Login card and the risk badge from the screen. During a 60-second allocation the lead can type a name and lose the only signal that ranks the queues. Suggested fix: keep the highest-risk queue, or a summary of it, visible above the filtered region.

findings.label: A
findings.description: All four queue cards render the same filled primary 'Reassign an agent here' button (renderQueueCard applies btn--primary unconditionally), so General — 95m against a 120m target, zero conversations due within ten minutes — offers as prominent an allocation action as Login. The visual risk cue is not carried into the action hierarchy. Suggested fix: make the primary action primary only on the at-risk queue and demote the rest to a secondary style.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The 'Highest near-term risk' badge is driven by isHighestRisk(q), which returns q.medianMinutes > q.targetMinutes alone. It ignores the due-within-10-minutes and arrival-spike facts the card itself cites as reasons, and it cannot rank, so a superlative label would attach to every over-target queue. It lands on the right queue with the supplied data by coincidence of the numbers. Suggested fix: derive the badge from a rank across the supplied risk facts, or rename it to state the rule it actually applies.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The document has two nested <main> landmarks — <main id="app"> in index.html plus <main class="page-body"> emitted by render() — which I confirmed at runtime (2 main elements). Heading structure also jumps from the h1 to the card h3s with no h2 in the default loaded state. Suggested fix: emit a single main landmark and promote the card headings or add a section heading level.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The error state asserts a cause the brief does not supply: 'The connection to the support platform timed out.' The scenario says nothing about an upstream platform or a timeout. It does not affect the allocation decision, so I did not treat it as a material unsupported fact, but it is invented detail in otherwise fact-disciplined copy. Suggested fix: state that queue data could not be loaded without naming a cause.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Undo exists only inside a toast on an 8000 ms timer (UNDO_WINDOW_MS; the timeout clears state.lastAction and re-renders). I verified at runtime that no Undo control remains nine seconds after a reassignment, and the assigned agent slot then shows only 'Assigned' with no unassign control. The brief states reassignment is reversible; after the window closes, the surface offers no way to reverse it. Suggested fix: keep a persistent reassignment record with its own undo, or add an unassign action to the assigned agent slot.

findings.label: B
findings.description: B surfaces Login's '+38% arrivals' note but drops the supplied counterpart fact that Billing, API, and General are within 10% of their prior-hour arrival counts.
