That fact is part of why Login is the outlier, and the table has no arrivals column at all, so the lead cannot see that the comparison is against steady queues. A shows 'Steady (within 10%)' on each non-spiking queue. Suggested fix: add an arrivals column or per-row note carrying the steady-state fact.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The shipped source/README.md is an unrelated starter stub ('An empty static starter: one HTML shell ... and an empty ES module') that describes neither the built surface nor how to reach the required states, while app.js cites FRAME.md, craft.md, and actions.md, none of which are in the packet. source/ also carries a stray artifacts/ directory of six build-time JPEGs. Suggested fix: replace the README with one documenting the ?state= flags and interactions, and drop the build artifacts from source/.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The two right-hand facts in the exception panel are circular: 'Agents on queue 3' is hinted '16 open conversations' and 'Open conversations 16' is hinted '3 agents assigned', so each tile's supporting line restates the other tile's headline. Suggested fix: replace one hint with a fact that adds information, such as the conversations-per-agent relation or the target comparison.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The comparison table's header cells are emitted as bare <th> with no scope attribute (renderZoneB); the only 'scope' string in app.js is an unrelated CSS class. The table is simple enough that implicit column association usually holds, but the association is left to the user agent. Suggested fix: set scope="col" on the header cells.

reviews.choice_reason: Both outputs identify Login as the queue at greatest near-term risk and preserve the supplied facts without invention. B better enables the 60-second allocation job on three concrete observations. (1) B leads with the answer: a 'Needs attention now' hero for Login with a single primary 'Reassign to Login' action and 'Login (recommended)' preselected in both agent assign controls, so the correct action is one click away; A presents four cards with identical primary 'Reassign an agent here' buttons on every queue, so the action layer itself does not privilege the at-risk queue — only the card tint does. (2) B's comparison table (open / agents / median vs. target / due ≤10 min) lets the lead verify the recommendation across queues in one scan; A requires reading four separately formatted cards. (3) Verified in a locally served run: B announces reassignment and undo through a persistent role=status polite live region ('Agent reassigned to Login. Login now has 4 agents...', 'Reassignment to Login undone.'), while A renders its confirmation tray with no aria-live/status/alert region present after the action, so the core interaction is silent for screen-reader users. A wins one dimension that B loses — A's undo persists in a 'Recent reassignments' tray while B's undo expires with an ~8-second toast (0 undo controls found 9.5s after reassigning) — but that does not outweigh B's faster path to the correct decision and stronger verified accessibility.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Reassignment and undo results are never announced to assistive technology. The only aria-live/role=status markup in the source is on the loading skeleton, and role=alert only on the error state; a live-DOM audit immediately after clicking 'Reassign an agent here' found zero [aria-live], [role=status], or [role=alert] elements, so the 'Recent reassignments' confirmation and the availability change are visual-only. For the core interaction of the surface this is a material accessibility gap.

findings.label: A
findings.description: All four queues carry an identical primary-styled 'Reassign an agent here' button, including Healthy-leaning General. The action hierarchy does not steer toward the at-risk queue at the point of action — distinction rests entirely on the Login card's tint and badge — and the packet's own interaction-01 capture reassigned an agent to Billing, illustrating how easily the first primary button absorbs the click.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Document structure defects: heading outline skips from H1 to H3 (no H2 level), and the source produces two <main> landmarks (live DOM audit reported main=2), which duplicates the primary landmark for assistive tech.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Undo exists only in a toast that expires: the status text says 'Undo available for 8 seconds', and a locally served run found 0 undo controls 9.5 seconds after reassigning, with no other reverse path on the surface. The brief states reassignment is reversible; a shift lead interrupted mid-task loses the ability to reverse. A's persistent 'Recent reassignments' tray handles this better.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The all-queues table's seven <th> header cells have no scope attributes, and the inline error banner is not marked role=alert, so header association and error announcement rely on browser heuristics.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The error state's user-facing copy reads "Couldn't load queue data (simulated network failure)" — the parenthetical leaks demo framing into production copy. Also the 'Watch'/'Healthy' status taxonomy has no visible legend or threshold definition, though the adjacent raw metrics keep the labels verifiable against supplied facts.

reviews.choice_reason: 1. B gives the 60-second decision a single unambiguous primary action ('Reassign to Login') plus per-agent 'Login (recommended)' dropdown defaults; A repeats an identical 'Reassign an agent here' label on all four cards with no default target, so the correct queue depends entirely on the user reading the highlighted card first — the packet's own replayable capture script, which grabs the first enabled reassign button, landed an agent on Billing (lower risk) instead of Login. 2. B announces reassign/undo outcomes through a persistent aria-live=polite region (announce() calls in source); A wires aria-live only to the loading skeleton, so a screen-reader user gets no confirmation a reassignment or undo succeeded. 3. B's 'Needs attention now' hero keeps the single highest-risk queue first in scroll order at both 1440px and 390px; A's equal-weight four-card grid places Login second, after Billing, at both sizes despite the color/badge treatment.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Every queue card has an identically-labeled 'Reassign an agent here' button with no globally recommended/default target. Under the scenario's 60-second budget this creates real risk of allocating an agent to the wrong (lower-risk) queue on a quick first click, rather than the highest-risk Login queue.

findings.label: A
findings.description: No aria-live announcement fires when a reassignment or undo completes — aria-live is wired only to the loading skeleton (app.js line 112), not to the reassign/undo code paths — so a screen-reader user has no non-visual confirmation that a time-critical action succeeded.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The inline error message includes the literal text '(simulated network failure)', leaking internal test/demo language into what should be realistic user-facing error copy.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The shipped README is generic, unmodified starter boilerplate ('An empty static starter: one HTML shell...') that does not describe this scenario, its required states, or interactions, unlike A's scenario-specific README.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The loading skeleton renders as generic full-width gray bars that do not preview the actual page structure (hero exception card, comparative table, agent list), giving weaker perceived-performance fidelity than a content-shaped skeleton.

findings.label: A
findings.description: At the 390px viewport the highlighted highest-risk Login card is the second card in scroll order, after Billing, so a shift lead must scroll past a lower-risk queue before reaching the one that needs action.

reviews.choice_reason: Within the stated four-minute budget, B puts the work in front of the director and A does not. In A, both case modules are content-free at rest — the desktop capture shows only 'Harbor Room / Community archive exhibition' and 'Night School / Public lecture series' above an 'Open the case' link — so scope and constraint require two interactions to reach, while the largest elements on the page are a self-descriptive headline plus a bordered contact panel with a red submit and a sticky red-underlined 'Start a conversation' bar. That inverts the scenario's own consequence note that fit must be visible through the work rather than generic self-description, and it puts the ask in competition with case evaluation. B's cards carry scope and constraint as running text before any click, and the dialog then adds Scope / Constraint / 'Outcome supplied' plus an explicit per-case line naming what was not supplied ('Attendance and revenue results were not supplied for this project.'; 'A client quote was not supplied for this project.'). Second, B marks the supplied/unsupplied boundary where the decision is actually made — per case, at the point of reading — whereas A carries a single global 'Not yet shared here' list buried inside the contact panel, so A's outcome lines read as unqualified claims at the moment the director evaluates them. Third, on the interaction I could verify by running both packages, B's case study is a native modal dialog that opens with focus moved to its close control, closes on Escape, and returns focus to the invoking button; A's successful submit hides the form and drops focus to document.body. A is the stronger artifact on two counts I weighed and did not treat as decisive: its typographic system is far more distinctive and internally coherent, and its contact form is the better-wired one (aria-describedby and aria-invalid maintained per field, which B omits entirely). Those raise A's D7 and D8 above B's but do not offset a page whose primary evidence is hidden behind clicks while its ask is the loudest thing on screen.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The case modules hold no evidence until interacted with. At rest each shows only a name, a one-line kicker, a two-letter mark, and an 'Open the case' control; scope, constraint, and outcome all sit behind a toggle. Against a four-minute budget and a brief whose consequence note says fit must be visible through the work rather than generic self-description, the director's first screen offers a self-descriptive headline and paragraph instead of the work. Evidence: A/desktop.png and A/source/index.html — .case__detail carries the hidden attribute and contains the entire dl of Scope/Constraint/Outcome. Suggested fix: surface scope and constraint as visible card text, and let the toggle reveal only the remaining detail.

findings.label: A
findings.description: A successful contact submission destroys the user's focus position. app.js sets form.hidden = true after a 400 ms delay, which removes the submit button that held focus; I confirmed in a locally served isolated Chromium run that document.activeElement is body afterwards. The success text is in a role=status live region so it is announced, but a keyboard or screen-reader user is returned to the top of the document with no landing point. Evidence: A/source/app.js initContactForm success branch; verified by running A/source with require('playwright'). Suggested fix: keep the confirmation in a focusable container and move focus to it rather than hiding the form outright.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Opening one case leaves a large empty field inside the sibling card. The two cases sit in a two-column grid whose rows stretch to equal height, so expanding Harbor Room stretches the collapsed Night School card to match, producing roughly 250 px of blank cream below its kicker. It reads as missing content rather than as a collapsed state. Evidence: A/evidence/interaction-01-open-a-case-study.png; A/source/styles.css .case grid. Suggested fix: set align-items: start on the .case grid.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The disclosure of what is not supplied is correct in substance but misplaced for the decision. 'Not yet shared here — Project pricing / Current availability / Awards and client list' sits inside the contact panel at the bottom of the page, so while the director is reading the two Outcome lines those lines carry no marker distinguishing a supplied outcome from an unmeasured one. B, by contrast, qualifies each case at the point of reading. Evidence: A/source/index.html .disclosure, placed inside section.contact. Suggested fix: mark the supplied/unsupplied boundary per case alongside the Outcome term as well as globally.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The focus indicator is a box-shadow with outline explicitly removed globally (*:focus-visible { outline: none; box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px var(--white), 0 0 0 5px var(--black) }). Box-shadow is not painted in Windows High Contrast / forced-colors mode, so keyboard focus becomes invisible for exactly the users most dependent on it. The ring is otherwise well-formed and clearly visible in the validation-error capture. Evidence: A/source/styles.css line ~94; A/evidence/state-01-contact-form-validation-error.png. Suggested fix: keep the box-shadow and restore a transparent outline of equal width so forced-colors substitutes a system color.

findings.label: B
findings.description: No contact field is programmatically associated with its error message. All four inputs lack aria-describedby entirely — I confirmed by reading the live DOM after an invalid submit that describedby is null on every control while the visible error text is present. The errors carry role=alert so they announce once when revealed, but a screen-reader user who tabs back to the organization field afterwards hears the label with no error attached, and aria-invalid is only added at submit time. A wires this correctly and B does not. Evidence: B/source/index.html fields; verified by running B/source in a locally launched isolated Chromium. Suggested fix: give each input a permanent aria-describedby pointing at its error paragraph.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The case-study dialog has no accessible name. #case-dialog carries neither aria-label nor aria-labelledby, and its heading is injected into #case-dialog-content at open time without being referenced, so the dialog announces as an unnamed modal. Focus handling itself is correct — I verified the dialog opens with focus on the close button, closes on Escape, and returns focus to the invoking 'Open case study' button. Evidence: B/source/index.html dialog markup and B/source/app.js renderCase; verified by running B/source. Suggested fix: set aria-labelledby to the injected case title, or aria-label to the case name at showModal time.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The hero overreaches on the one line where the page is otherwise scrupulous. 'not a summary of results that were never measured' converts 'no result was supplied' into an assertion that no measurement occurred. Everywhere else B is precise — the work-section note, the per-case unsupplied lines, and the process caveat all say 'not supplied.' Evidence: B/source/index.html .hero-sub; B/desktop.png. Suggested fix: match the wording used elsewhere on the page.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The primary action is under-labelled at the point of commitment and duplicated above it. The section heading and the header pill both read 'Request a project conversation,' but the button that performs it says only 'Send,' which is the least specific label on the page and the one the director actually presses. Correctly, no response time is promised anywhere. Evidence: B/source/index.html .submit-button; B/desktop.png. Suggested fix: label the button with the action, e.g. 'Request a conversation.'

findings.label: B
findings.description: The form-status region distinguishes success but not failure. app.js sets status.dataset.state to 'error' or 'success', and styles.css defines a color only for [data-state='success']; the error message 'Fix the highlighted fields before sending.' renders in default body ink at 0.9rem below the button, visually indistinguishable from ordinary copy. The per-field errors do carry the accent color, so the state is recoverable. Evidence: B/source/styles.css .form-status rules; B/evidence/state-01-contact-form-validation-error.png. Suggested fix: give data-state='error' the same treatment as the field errors.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The modal presentation means the two cases can never be seen together. Each opens over the page and the other is dimmed behind it, so comparing Harbor Room against Night School requires holding one in memory. With only two cases this is minor, and the cards' visible summaries partly compensate; A's inline expansion is the better model on this one point. Evidence: B/evidence/interaction-01-open-a-case-study.png. Suggested fix: consider inline expansion, or repeat the comparable terms on the card face.

reviews.choice_reason: The job is a museum program director deciding fit for identity and wayfinding work, where the brief's own acceptance check says the work itself must be the strongest evidence. A's page is itself a demonstration of exhibition-identity craft — a confident constructivist poster system with a coherent type, color, and border language — while B is a tasteful but generic editorial layout that demonstrates far less of the capability being commissioned. Second, both outputs honestly separate supplied outcomes from unsupplied commercial claims, but A does it in-world ('Not yet shared here … These come up in the conversation, not on this page') while B leaks evaluation-frame language into visitor-facing copy ('Outcome supplied', 'they were not supplied', 'not a summary of results that were never measured'), which reads oddly to the stated role and in one place overreaches the brief. Third, A's contact form has the strongest inspectable interaction evidence: per-field errors wired with aria-invalid plus aria-describedby, an error summary, and a budget-range select that scaffolds the required details, versus B's unlinked error text and free-text budget field. B is genuinely better in two respects — its case cards surface scope and constraint directly on the landing view, and its native <dialog> case detail gets focus trapping and Escape handling for free — but its case 'study' modal only repeats the card content plus one outcome line, so the depth advantage A offers on expansion outweighs it.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Evaluation-frame language leaks into visitor-facing copy in at least four places: hero ('the outcome supplied for each — not a summary of results that were never measured'), case-section intro ('Where a result … was not supplied, it is not shown here'), process footnote ('they were not supplied'), and the case dialog ('Attendance and revenue results were not supplied for this project', heading 'Outcome supplied'). 'Supplied' addresses the packet reviewer, not a museum program director; the voice undermines the persuasive job and 'never measured' overreaches the brief. Evidence: B desktop.png, B interaction-01, B source app.js caseData strings.

findings.label: A
findings.description: After a successful submit, the button stays disabled with label 'Sending…' while the status line already reads 'Your project details were sent.' — two contradictory states shown at once at the page's primary action. Evidence: A interaction-03 screenshot; A app.js sets the label to 'Sending…' and the setTimeout success handler updates only the status text, never the button label.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Field validation messages are rendered adjacent to inputs but never programmatically associated with them — the source contains no aria-describedby anywhere, so a screen-reader user tabbing into an invalid field hears 'invalid' (aria-invalid is set) but not the specific guidance text. Evidence: B source index.html and app.js (0 aria-describedby occurrences; error elements referenced only by id for textContent updates).

findings.label: B
findings.description: 'Open case study' opens a modal that contains only the card's existing scope/constraint text plus one outcome sentence — the promised case-study depth is a single new line, and the modal blocks side-by-side comparison of the two cases while open. For a 4-minute evaluation this is an interaction cost without an information payoff. Evidence: B interaction-01 versus B desktop.png card copy; renderCase() in B app.js.

findings.label: A
findings.description: On the desktop landing view the case cards show only title and kicker ('Harbor Room — Community archive exhibition'); scope, constraint, and outcome are hidden until 'Open the case' is clicked. B surfaces scope and constraint directly on the cards, giving faster scent within the 4-minute budget. A's expansion is one click and inline, so the cost is small, but the initial cards under-inform. Evidence: A desktop.png versus A interaction-01.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Header brand and the 'Start a conversation' link are not wrapped in a nav landmark (0 <nav> elements in A's markup; B has one). Skip link, main landmark, heading order, aria-expanded/aria-controls on disclosures, and a reduced-motion kill switch are all present, so the gap is isolated. Evidence: A source index.html.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The budget-range select invents four specific dollar bands not present in the brief's closed fact set. As an input affordance with a 'Not yet set' option it stops short of asserting Mara's pricing, but the bands imply a pricing frame no fact supports; a neutral free-text field (as B uses) or unlabeled ranges would be safer. Evidence: A desktop.png, A source index.html option elements.

reviews.choice_reason: 1. B's case-study cards show a one-line scope/outcome summary directly on the collapsed card, so the director gets real project evidence before any click; A's collapsed cards show only a title, kicker, and 'Open the case' button, requiring an interaction before any project-specific evidence is visible at all — a real cost against the brief's stated 4-minute time budget. 2. B's contact form asks for budget range as free text; A's budget field is a <select> with specific invented dollar bands (Under $10,000 / $10,000-25,000 / $25,000-75,000 / $75,000+) that the scenario brief explicitly says were not supplied — this edges toward implying typical price tiers for the designer's work. 3. B's case-study detail uses a native <dialog> (showModal), giving robust built-in focus handling and Escape-to-close for free; A's inline accordion is also correctly implemented (aria-expanded/aria-controls) but trades that off against point 1 above.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Collapsed case-study cards expose no project content beyond the title and kicker phrase — scope, constraint, and outcome are only visible after clicking 'Open the case.' Given the brief's stated 4-minute time budget for a director to judge fit, this forces an extra interaction before any real evidence is visible, versus B which surfaces a one-line project summary on the card itself.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The budget-range field is a <select> with specific invented dollar bands (Under $10,000 / $10,000-25,000 / $25,000-75,000 / $75,000 and above). The scenario brief states 'typical project length, price, availability, awards, and client list are not supplied' — presenting concrete price tiers on the page, even as client-facing intake categories, risks reading as an implicit signal of the designer's typical rates that the brief withholds.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Case-study detail opens in a full-screen native modal dialog. Comparing Harbor Room and Night School requires closing one dialog before opening the other, adding friction to a quick side-by-side read, whereas A's in-place accordion leaves the sibling case card visible while one is expanded.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Full-page evidence screenshots (interaction-03, state-01, state-02) show the sticky black utility bar duplicated mid-page, overlapping content such as the 'Production handoff' row. Source shows .utility-bar uses position:sticky/top:0, and capture-plan.mjs takes Playwright screenshots with fullPage:true, which is known to stitch fixed/sticky elements repeatedly across tall captures. This looks like a capture-tooling artifact rather than a live rendering bug, but it cannot be fully ruled out from stills alone.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The same duplicated sticky-header artifact appears in B's full-page evidence (interaction-02, state-01, state-02), overlapping case-card and section content. B's .site-header also uses position:sticky/top:0 and its capture script also uses fullPage:true screenshots, so this is most likely the same shared capture-tooling artifact as in A, not a differentiating defect.

reviews.choice_reason: B answers the operations lead's actual question in the first screen: the headline reads '35 members on Team costs $420 per month, or $4,200 per year', with both totals shown simultaneously and recomputed from the seat field, so neither arithmetic nor an interaction is required to see either cadence. A reaches the same numbers but shows only the selected cadence's total inside the Team card, so the annual figure requires toggling first. Second, B degrades correctly at the edges of the fact set: when the seat count exceeds Team's 100-member cap, app.js reveals a note disqualifying Team on the claim itself and strikes the price, whereas A's Team card keeps rendering a live-looking per-month total for a seat count Team cannot serve, contradicting its own recommendation text lower on the page. Third, at 390 px B reflows the plan matrix into per-criterion stacked groups where every plan's value stays visible, while A keeps a wide table inside an overflow-x container — in A's own 390 px capture the Team and Enterprise columns are clipped off-screen, so the comparison that acceptance check 2 depends on is not legible without horizontal scrolling. B also supplies the contact-sales affordance the brief names as the appropriate next action for an Enterprise-bound visitor; A only mentions contacting sales in prose with no control. This choice is made in spite of B's factual defects, not in ignorance of them: B asserts two capabilities the brief does not supply (see unsupported_claims), and those must be fixed. They are peripheral to a 35-person Starter-vs-Team decision, whereas A's mobile clipping and over-cap price sit directly on the decision path. A's comparison table is genuinely the stronger artifact on desktop — it carries cancellation, mid-period seat changes, and per-plan trial terms, and it uses 'Not stated' rather than inventing Enterprise details.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The Team card renders a live, confident total for any seat count, including counts above Team's 100-member cap. pricing/app.js renderTeamPricing() multiplies the per-member rate by the seat count with no cap check, so entering 150 in the member-count field yields '$1,800 / month for 150 members' in the primary price position while the recommendation paragraph further down says Enterprise is the appropriate plan. A visitor who reads the card and not the paragraph takes away a price for a plan that cannot serve them. Evidence: source/pricing/app.js lines 35-55 (no cap branch) versus renderRecommendation() lines 57-70 (which does branch on TEAM_MEMBER_CAP). Suggested fix: gate the Team total on the cap and mark Team as disqualified in the card itself when the seat count exceeds 100, matching what the recommendation already says.

findings.label: A
findings.description: At 390 px the plan-differences table is clipped rather than reflowed. pricing/styles.css wraps it in .table-scroll { overflow-x: auto }, and the responsive rules at 720 px and 420 px restack the plan cards but leave the table's column structure untouched. In A's own state-03-390-px-viewport.png only the Detail and Starter columns are readable; the Team column is cut at the right edge and Enterprise is entirely off-screen, with no visible scroll affordance indicating more columns exist. Acceptance check 2 asks that plan differences, limits, cadence, and cancellation terms stay legible, and on a phone they do not. Suggested fix: reflow the table to per-criterion stacked groups below ~640 px, or at minimum add a persistent scroll cue and freeze the Detail column.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The brief names two appropriate next actions for an undecided visitor — start a trial, or contact sales for Enterprise — and A ships a control for only the first. The Enterprise card's action slot holds the static text 'Contact sales' as a fit line (source/pricing/index.html line 113), not a link or button, and the recommendation paragraph likewise says 'contact sales for pricing' as prose. A visitor whose organization needs SAML SSO or SCIM reaches the end of the page with no affordance to act on. Suggested fix: give the Enterprise card a real contact-sales control equivalent in weight to the Team trial button.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Two matrix cells state capabilities the closed fact set does not supply: Enterprise 'Unlimited workspaces' and a 'Support contact' row giving Starter and Team a 'Standard' tier. Evidence: source/index.html Workspaces and Support contact rows, visible in desktop.png and state-03-390-px-viewport.png. Both read as authoritative product facts in a comparison intended to drive a purchase decision. Suggested fix: replace the Enterprise workspaces cell with 'Not stated — ask sales' as B already does in the Member cap row, and drop the Support contact row entirely, folding the named implementation contact into the Enterprise 'Included' cell where the brief actually places it.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The comparison matrix is materially thinner than the decision requires. Cancellation timing and the mid-period seat-change caveat appear only in the Zone B terms list, far below the matrix, and Slack links and admin roles are collapsed into a prose 'Included' cell rather than given comparable rows. A reader scanning the matrix to answer 'what exactly do I lose by staying on Starter' has to reconstruct the answer from a comma-separated string, and cancellation terms are not adjacent to the price they qualify. Evidence: source/index.html matrix (6 rows) versus the 14-row table in A. Suggested fix: keep the terms section but add cancellation as a matrix row so cadence and exit terms sit together.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The comparison table mixes two different epistemic conventions in the same columns without distinguishing them. Team's Handoff template and CSV export cells read 'Not stated', but Team's SAML SSO, SCIM, and Audit export cells read a definitive 'No', and Starter's Slack links and Admin roles read 'No' — all of these are the same kind of gap in the brief (a feature listed for one plan and not for another). The reader cannot tell whether 'No' means confirmed absence or the same unknown that 'Not stated' marks. Evidence: source/pricing/index.html table rows, lines 154-231. Suggested fix: pick one convention for unlisted features and apply it uniformly across all three plans.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The trial form validates only that a work email is non-empty and matches a loose pattern, and on success it disables both the field and the button. There is no seat-count carry-through from the calculator into the trial, so the seat figure the visitor just reasoned about is discarded at the moment of commitment, and the success message states the trial started with no way to correct a mistyped address. Evidence: source/app.js lines 118-138. Suggested fix: carry the calculated seat count into the trial submission and leave an edit path after the success state.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The page's most valuable sentence — the concrete total for this team's headcount — is set as small supporting text ('$420 / month for 35 members') beneath a large '$12 / member / month' that the visitor already knew. The typographic emphasis is on the unit rate rather than on the committed amount the operations lead has to defend. Evidence: desktop.png, Team card; pricing/styles.css .plan-price .amount versus .plan-total. Suggested fix: promote the headcount total to the dominant figure in the Team card and demote the per-member rate to the qualifier.

reviews.choice_reason: B answers the operations lead's core question — what 35 members on Team actually costs — in the page headline ($420/month or $4,200/year) with zero interaction required, and the highlight tracks the billing toggle state. B also provides working controls for both sanctioned next actions (Start Team trial button and a real Contact sales button), while A renders 'Contact sales' as inert paragraph text with no affordance. At 390px, B restructures the comparison into stacked per-criterion groups that stay fully legible, whereas A's 14-row table has min-width 640px and requires horizontal scroll, appearing clipped in the capture. A is stricter on the closed fact set — its 'Not stated' discipline is exemplary and B invents two table cells (Enterprise 'Unlimited workspaces', 'Standard' support tier) — but those inventions sit in rows that do not distort the core Starter-vs-Team-vs-Enterprise decision for a 35-person team, while A's gaps directly slow the stated job. Both give a supported fit reason with no popularity claims. Evidence viewed: desktop, 390px states, interaction and state captures, sanitized source for both.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Invented material fact: Enterprise 'Unlimited workspaces' in the comparison table is not in the scenario's closed fact set. In a persuade-mode page this could steer an Enterprise evaluation on a capability the vendor never stated. Fix: replace with 'Not stated — ask sales' as the same table already does for the Enterprise member cap.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Invented support tier: 'Support contact: Standard' for Starter and Team is unsupplied. Lower stakes than the workspaces cell because it implies a vague default rather than a specific capability, but it still asserts a policy the facts do not contain. Fix: mark as not stated or drop the row except for Enterprise's named contact.

findings.label: A
findings.description:
The Enterprise path has no actionable control: 'Contact sales' is a plain

with no link or button (pricing/index.html line 113). The brief names contacting sales as one of the two appropriate next actions for an undecided visitor, and the recommendation copy itself says 'contact sales for pricing' — but there is nothing to activate. Fix: make it a button or mailto-style link, mirroring the trial CTA.

findings.label: A
findings.description: At 390px the Plan differences table (min-width: 640px inside .table-scroll with overflow-x: auto) requires horizontal scrolling and appears clipped mid-column in the capture, straining the acceptance check that plan differences remain legible. The 14-row table is the page's only complete feature comparison. Fix: collapse to a stacked per-criterion layout at narrow widths, as B demonstrates.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The answer to the visitor's central question — what 35 members costs — is not surfaced at the top level. The headline is generic ('Choose the right plan for your team') and the $420/month figure sits inside the Team card below the calculator; the annual figure appears only after operating the toggle. The information is present and correct, but the hierarchy makes the user assemble it rather than presenting it.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The Monthly/Annual control uses a two-sided switch with labels on both flanks, a pattern whose selected side can read ambiguously from the knob alone. Mitigated here: the aria-label updates to 'Billing: Monthly/Annual selected', the headline highlight moves with the state, and the table price cell switches cadence. Polish-level only.

reviews.choice_reason: 1. B's plan-differences table restructures into legible stacked label/value blocks at the required 390px viewport (verified in state-03-390-px-viewport.png and the max-width:640px media query in source/styles.css), while A's table relies on horizontal overflow scroll with min-width:640px and no visible scroll affordance, cutting off two of three plan columns at 390px — a direct miss against the brief's acceptance check that plan differences must remain legible. 2. B's headline claim always shows both the monthly and annual totals for the entered team size ($420/month or $4,200/year for 35 members) so the exact Team cost is visible without toggling or mental arithmetic, and the same claim self-disqualifies Team (claim-disqualified state, verified in source) when seat count exceeds the 100-member cap; A only shows the currently selected cadence and its Team price card has no such disqualification logic for over-cap sizes (verified by absence of an overCap branch in renderTeamPricing()). 3. B gives the Enterprise path — one of the two 'appropriate next actions' named in the brief — an actionable Contact Sales button with a captured click-confirmation state, while A presents 'Contact sales' as static text with no interactive affordance.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The 'Plan differences' table does not restructure for narrow viewports. It sits in a .table-scroll (overflow-x:auto) container with table min-width:640px and no responsive breakpoint that reflows it, so at the required 390px viewport only the Detail and Starter columns are visible; Team and Enterprise are pushed off-screen with only a text sliver showing and no visible scroll cue in the screenshot. This directly conflicts with the acceptance check that plan differences, limits, billing cadence, and cancellation terms remain legible.

findings.label: A
findings.description:
The Enterprise plan card's 'Contact sales' is a plain

text node with no href/button/click handler, unlike the Team card's explicit 'Start a Team trial' button. Since the brief states the appropriate next action for an undecided visitor is 'to start a trial or contact sales,' the second of those two actions has no affordance to actually perform it.

findings.label: A
findings.description: renderTeamPricing() computes and displays a Team per-member price and total for any entered member count with no over-cap branch; only the separate 'Which plan fits' recommendation text (not the price claim itself) tells an over-100-member visitor Team doesn't fit. Not demonstrated in the provided screenshots (default input is 35), but the gap is visible in source and would let an over-cap visitor see a live-looking Team price on the primary price claim.

findings.label: A
findings.description: CSS defines a visible :focus-visible outline on the billing radios, but the evidence capture script exercises the 'keyboard interaction' state via page.focus() + ArrowRight (a programmatic focus call) rather than a real Tab press, and the resulting screenshot shows no visible focus ring on either pill. Real Tab-order reachability of the control is not demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The primary 'Start Team Trial' / 'Contact Sales' call-to-action buttons and the inline field-error text both use the same red hue, reducing the color's usefulness as a distinct semantic signal for errors versus primary actions in a persuade/decision context.

reviews.choice_reason: B better enables a support operations leader to decide about a 14-day trial in two minutes. First, the brief names migration effort as the primary objection, and B answers it in visible page content: a titled 'Bringing your incident log over' block stating CSV import plus guided template setup, an expandable three-step import detail, and an explicit note that no typical import duration has been published. In A the entire migration answer sits behind a plain underlined text link ('See how CSV import works', A/source/index.html:40-42) whose target section is hidden by default (A/source/index.html:94 `hidden`), so a reader who does not click never encounters the answer to the decisive objection — and A's default-state page (A/desktop.png) is a hero and a stranded footer button with a large empty region, giving no signal that further content exists. Second, on evidence adjacency, B places the qualified 31-to-9 figure, the explicit 'This is one customer case, not a universal claim' qualifier, and the approved Priya Nair testimonial together in visible content (B/desktop.png, B/source/index.html:167-192); A shows only a summarized metric with a qualifier and hides the testimonial and full case behind a disclosure (A/source/index.html:72-92). Third, on inspectable interaction quality, B ships a skip link (B/source/index.html:14), a global :focus-visible rule (B/source/styles.css:132), disclosure panels placed immediately after their controlling buttons, and a reduced-motion block that also neutralizes scroll-behavior (B/source/styles.css:89-98); A has no skip link, styles focus only on the email input (A/source/styles.css:204), and its one motion effect is a JS scrollIntoView({behavior:'smooth'}) (A/source/app.js:11) that its CSS reduced-motion block (A/source/styles.css:277-283, transitions and animations only) does not and cannot cover, so A's reduced-motion state is not honored for the only animation it has. A's genuine advantage is that its trial form sits above the fold at 1440x900 while B requires a scroll or an anchor click to reach the form; that is real but does not outweigh a buried objection answer, buried proof, and a hollow default page.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The answer to the scenario's stated primary objection is invisible in the default state. Migration content lives in section#csv-panel, which carries the hidden attribute (A/source/index.html:94) and is revealed only by a plain underlined text link styled like body copy (A/source/index.html:40-42, .link-btn in A/source/styles.css:98-108). A/desktop.png confirms the default page is a hero plus a stranded footer button with roughly a third of the viewport empty and no section headings, so nothing signals that migration, the case detail, or the testimonial exist below. Within a two-minute budget a reader can plausibly finish the page having seen neither the import mechanism nor the approved testimonial. Fix: surface at least a short migration block and the testimonial as visible content, and reserve disclosure for the detail beneath them.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The success state asserts an unsupplied outcome: "We'll email {address} to confirm your 14-day workspace." (A/source/app.js:58). No confirmation-email behavior is in the brief, and the static build cannot perform it. Because this appears at the moment of commitment it shapes the reader's expectation of what starting a trial actually does. Fix: confirm only what the build did (a captured request) or restate supplied terms, as the parallel handling in B/source/app.js:69-70 does.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The required reduced-motion state is not actually honored. A's only motion is panel.scrollIntoView({ behavior: "smooth" }) in A/source/app.js:11; the reduced-motion media query at A/source/styles.css:277-283 overrides transition-duration, animation-duration, and animation-iteration-count only, none of which affect a JS-specified smooth scroll. A user with prefers-reduced-motion still gets an animated scroll on every disclosure open. The supplied evidence cannot show this: A/evidence/state-02-reduced-motion-preference.png is byte-identical (sha1 d95408d3) to A/desktop.png, so it captures the page at rest rather than the motion in question. Fix: read window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') and pass behavior 'auto' when it matches.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Keyboard and screen-reader affordances are thinner than the markup otherwise suggests. There is no skip link; the only focus style in the stylesheet is on #work-email (A/source/styles.css:204-207), leaving every button and link on the user-agent default; and when a disclosure opens, focus stays on the toggle while the page scrolls elsewhere (A/source/app.js:6-13), so a keyboard user is moved visually without being moved in the focus order. The disclosure semantics themselves are correct — aria-expanded and aria-controls are set and kept in sync, and the error uses role="alert" with aria-invalid — so this is degradation, not absence. Fix: add a skip link, a shared :focus-visible rule, and move focus to the revealed panel.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The default composition leaves substantial unresolved space and a redundant terminal action. In A/desktop.png the right column ends at the trial card with roughly 450px of empty canvas beneath it, and the footer 'Start trial' button (A/source/index.html:113) is an anchor to #trial-form — a form that is visible on the same screen, directly above it. The result reads as an unfinished page rather than a deliberately short one. Fix: either let the case and migration content occupy that space or drop the footer CTA, which cannot earn its place while the form is already in view.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Internal authoring scaffolding ships in the production markup: data-zone attributes on sections, data-el="C1,C2" / "E1"–"E8" on elements, data-action="S1" on CTAs, and HTML comments phrased as numbered design questions (B/source/index.html:16, 28, 33-34, 37, 40, 46, 61, 93-96, 103, 132, 144, 159, 166-167, 170, 200, 226, 243, 249). None of it affects rendering or assistive technology, but it is process residue in a shipped artifact and, in a review context, it partially telegraphs how the page was made. Fix: strip the attributes and comments at build time.

findings.label: B
findings.description: On successful submit the handler sets the submit button's disabled property (B/source/app.js:71). A keyboard user whose focus is on that button loses it to document.body, so the confirmation in .form-status is announced via aria-live but the user's place in the page is gone and the next Tab restarts from the top. Fix: keep the button enabled and rely on the status message, or move focus to the status element before disabling.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Two claims run slightly ahead of the supplied facts: "Relay Notes has one published case so far" (B/source/index.html:219-220), which converts the brief's scoping caveat into an assertion about the company's published evidence; and the framing "The biggest question before switching tools is usually what happens to the incident history you already have" (B/source/index.html:133-134), which generalizes the brief's statement that migration effort is this reader's primary objection into a claim about buyers at large. Neither fabricates proof and both push toward understatement, but they are assertions the closed fact set does not license. Fix: scope both to the supplied case and this reader.

findings.label: B
findings.description: At 390px the offer section develops an unexplained vertical gap between the work-email input and the 'Start your trial' button (B/mobile.png, lower third) where the desktop row layout unstacks. The controls remain legible, ordered, and reachable, so this is polish rather than friction. Fix: normalize the stacked field-to-button spacing in the max-width 480px block.

reviews.choice_reason: B better enables a support operations leader to decide on the trial within the two-minute budget. (1) B makes the product mechanism concrete: the five handoff fields (owner, customer impact, latest decision, next step, linked evidence) are each named and explained, and the hero sidebar summarizes the record — directly serving the fit assessment the consequence statement demands, whereas A names the fields only once in a sentence. (2) B's evidence handling is stronger: the 31→9 Brightline stat appears with its one-customer qualification adjacent in both the hero and the case section, and the 'Inspect the Brightline case' disclosure reveals a structured before/after/what-this-covers breakdown (evidence/interaction-02). (3) B answers the stated migration objection with three concrete import steps behind 'See how CSV import works' (evidence/interaction-03), while A offers two short prose paragraphs. (4) A's valid-submit path asserts an invented confirmation flow ('We'll email {value} to confirm your 14-day workspace'), while B's source deliberately reports only what the static build can do. A's above-the-fold inline form is a genuine strength for action clarity, but it does not outweigh B's advantage on the decision itself.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The success state after a valid email submit asserts 'We'll email {value} to confirm your 14-day workspace' — an invented confirmation flow not in the scenario facts and not something the build performs. This misleads the evaluator about what happens next at the single point of commitment. Evidence: source/app.js submit handler. Fix: report only what is supported, e.g. confirm the request was captured without promising an email.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Three identical 'Start trial' CTAs render on one 1440x900 screen (nav pill, form button, and a floating centered button in the otherwise empty lower half of the page), and the lower-left region of the desktop layout is largely blank. The floating third CTA sits detached from any content and weakens hierarchy. Evidence: desktop.png. Fix: remove the floating duplicate or anchor it to a content section.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The product mechanism is thin for a fit-evaluation audience: the five handoff fields are named once in the hero sentence and once in the case panel prose, with no per-field explanation. An ops leader weighing training/migration cost gets little to assess about what the record actually contains. Evidence: desktop.png, source/index.html visible text. Fix: give the five fields a scannable breakdown.

findings.label: A
findings.description: No skip link and no :focus-visible differentiation (a single generic :focus rule in styles.css). Error handling is otherwise well wired (label/for, aria-invalid, aria-describedby, role=alert, focus moved to the field — source/app.js). Evidence: source/styles.css, source/index.html. Fix: add a skip link and :focus-visible styles.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The hero 'Start your trial' CTA anchors to the trial form at the very bottom of a long page (all hrefs point to #trial-form in the footer section). The distance between the commitment click and the form is large, and on mobile (390px) the form is a long scroll away. The skip link and nav CTA mitigate but do not remove the travel cost. Evidence: source/index.html hrefs, mobile.png. Fix: consider a compact inline email capture in the hero or a sticky CTA.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The section heading 'See the handoff, live' overpromises: what follows is a static five-field list, nothing live or interactive. Wording polish, not a factual invention. Evidence: desktop.png. Fix: retitle, e.g. 'What a handoff contains.'

reviews.choice_reason: 1. B's zone-structured page (hero, mechanism, case, offer) directly answers the six audience questions implied by the brief — including a step-by-step CSV import explanation and a detailed before/after breakdown of the Brightline case — while staying inside the supplied facts, giving the support-ops leader more decision-relevant context per section than A's terser inline disclosures. 2. A's trial-submit success message states 'We'll email {address} to confirm your 14-day workspace' — a confirmation-email process not present anywhere in the scenario facts — while B's equivalent success state ('Trial request captured in this demo...') stays honest about what a static build can verify; this is a material fidelity gap for A under D1/D6. 3. A's desktop and mobile layouts leave a large empty gap between the collapsed-panel hero and a floating duplicate 'Start trial' button, reading as a layout defect, whereas B's sections flow continuously with consistent visual identity (the same owner/impact/decision/next-step/evidence dot system repeated between hero and mechanism zone) and additional accessibility scaffolding (skip link, global focus-visible outline) not present in A.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Trial-form success state asserts an unsupported capability: 'We'll email {work-email} to confirm your 14-day workspace.' Evidence: A/source/app.js lines 57-59 (formSuccess.textContent). No supplied fact describes a confirmation email; the scenario only supplies trial length, work-email requirement, no-credit-card, and admin-deletable workspaces. This materially misleads a reader evaluating what actually happens after signup. Suggested fix: replace with a claim scoped to what the static build can verify, e.g. B's pattern ('Trial request captured in this demo...').

findings.label: A
findings.description: Desktop and mobile screenshots show a large empty vertical gap between the hero content (with collapsed case/CSV panels) and a duplicate floating 'Start trial' button near the bottom of the page, before the page ends with no visible footer content. Evidence: A/desktop.png, A/mobile.png. Reads as an unintended layout/spacing defect rather than a deliberate second CTA placement. Suggested fix: either anchor the secondary CTA directly under the hero content or remove it, and confirm panel expand/collapse doesn't leave orphaned whitespace when both panels are closed.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Only the work-email input has a custom focus style (styles.css line 204-207: '#work-email:focus'); no skip link and no focus-visible rule for other interactive elements (toggle buttons, CTA links). Keyboard users get browser-default focus indication elsewhere rather than a deliberate, consistent one. Evidence: A/source/styles.css (1 total :focus rule) vs B/source/styles.css (skip-link plus a global :focus-visible rule). Not disqualifying since defaults still render a visible outline, but less deliberate than B's treatment. Suggested fix: add a project-wide :focus-visible rule and a skip-to-content link.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Full page requires substantially more scrolling than A — the mobile capture is roughly 3340px tall against A's roughly 2200px — against a stated 2-minute time budget for the role. Evidence: B/mobile.png vs A/mobile.png. The extra content (mechanism zone, detailed case breakdown) is relevant and fact-supported, but the added length works against the stated time constraint. Suggested fix: consider condensing the mechanism zone or making the case detail the only expandable section, since its content duplicates the hero proof-strip stat.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Shipped markup contains data-el/data-zone/data-action attributes with no corresponding behavior in app.js or styles.css (e.g. data-el="C1,C2" on the header). These appear to be leftover build/annotation instrumentation rather than intentional application code. Evidence: B/source/index.html lines 16, 34, 61, 96, 103, 132, 138-146, 167, 194-203, 227, 243, 249. Not user-visible and not an accessibility defect, but adds noise to the shipped source. Suggested fix: strip non-functional data-* attributes before shipping the build.

reviews.choice_reason: Both outputs present the same five notes faithfully and both let a release engineer find the breaking retention change and its existing-project exception quickly, so the decision turned on which one holds up when the engineer actually operates it. Three verified behaviours separate them. First, copy honesty: I served each source/ locally and drove it with a locally launched isolated Chromium (require('playwright') above the checkout), stubbed navigator.clipboard.writeText to reject and forced document.execCommand to return false. A's confirmation then reads "Couldn't copy — select the retentionDays value above instead", while B still reports "Copied" on the button and "Copied 'retentionDays'" in its live region — a false success in exactly the state where the engineer believes retentionDays is on the clipboard and pastes something else into relay.config.json. Second, the primary jump action: with a filter active that hides the breaking note (query "dry-run"), A clears the filter and moves focus to the breaking section (document.activeElement = SECTION#note-breaking), whereas B's jump leaves focus on BODY and the breaking note stays hidden, so the one action the scenario names most explicitly fails silently mid-search. Third, findability: searching the word "breaking" returns 1 note in A and 0 in B, because B's data-search index is built only from the title and body and never includes the note type. A also gives the breaking note a genuinely different weight — tinted panel, an explicitly labelled "Existing-project exception" callout, a legend whose markers differ in shape as well as colour, and a "1 breaking change · 1 changed · 1 added · 1 fixed · 1 deprecated" count line — so the applicable change and its exception land in one scan. B is better in two respects worth recording: its H2s are descriptive sentences rather than bare type words, which makes heading-based screen-reader navigation more useful, and its configuration reference is a real navigable placeholder page at the specified /changelog/3.4.0/ route rather than an in-page anchor. Those advantages do not outweigh a confirmation that lies about the clipboard, a jump that no-ops, and a 224 px empty region on mobile.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The copy confirmation reports success unconditionally. wireCopyButtons() awaits navigator.clipboard.writeText inside a try, falls back to a textarea plus document.execCommand in the catch, and then sets the button text to "Copied" and unhides the aria-live confirmation regardless of whether either path worked; the execCommand return value is discarded. I confirmed this in a locally launched isolated browser by making writeText reject and execCommand return false: the button still read "Copied" and the live region announced "Copied 'retentionDays'". A release engineer in a locked-down or non-secure-context browser is told the key is on the clipboard when it is not, and the next paste into relay.config.json carries whatever was there before. Fix: capture the outcome of both paths and render a failure message that points at the visible retentionDays code element, as the clipboard write result is already available.

findings.label: B
findings.description: "Jump to breaking changes" silently does nothing while a search filter is hiding the breaking note. wireJumpFocus() waits 300 ms, then calls focus() on #breaking-retention; because the filter sets note.hidden, the element is display:none and focus() is a no-op. Verified locally: with the query "dry-run" active, clicking the jump link left document.activeElement on BODY and the breaking note stayed hidden, with no message explaining why. Filtering and then reaching for the breaking note is a natural sequence under a five-minute budget, and the failure gives the engineer no signal that anything was suppressed. Fix: clear the active filter (or re-show the target) before moving focus, and announce that the search was cleared.

findings.label: B
findings.description: At 390 px the header carries roughly 183 px of dead whitespace between the search field and the first note, pushing the breaking change further below the fold on the viewport where scanning is most expensive. Cause is verifiable in the source: .toolbar switches to flex-direction: column under the max-width: 480px query while .search keeps flex: 1 1 14rem, so the 14 rem basis is applied to height rather than width. Measured in a locally launched browser at 390 px: .search resolves to 224 px tall around a 41 px input, and the header is 471 px tall. The supplied 390 px state screenshot shows the same void. Fix: reset the search flex basis (for example flex: 0 0 auto or flex-basis: auto) inside the mobile media query.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The custom "Clear" control collides with the browser's native search-input clear affordance. The input is type="search" and the .search__clear button is absolutely positioned inside the same relatively positioned wrapper, so once text is present both render in the same spot; the supplied no-results state screenshot shows the glyph and the word overlapping as "✕Clear". Two overlapping clear controls in the same few pixels is an ambiguous target and looks unfinished at the exact moment the reader is trying to recover from an empty result. Fix: suppress the native decoration with input[type=search]::-webkit-search-cancel-button { -webkit-appearance: none }, or drop the custom button and rely on the native one.

findings.label: B
findings.description: In-page search cannot find a note by its type. The data-search attribute is composed from title, body, callout, and configHelp only, so the label words are indexed only where they happen to appear in prose. Verified locally: the query "breaking" returns 0 of 5 notes even though a breaking change exists and the page displays a BREAKING chip, while "deprecated" returns 1 only because the word appears in that note's title. An engineer who types the category word they can see on screen gets B's no-results panel and may conclude the release has no breaking change. Fix: include note.type and note.label in the indexed string.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Every note heading is a bare type word — the H2 outline reads "Note type key, Breaking, Changed, Added, Fixed, Deprecated, Configuration reference". A screen-reader user navigating by heading, which is the fastest way to triage a release under time pressure, learns only the category of each note and must enter each one to discover what changed. B's descriptive headings (for example "Default artifact retention is now 30 days for new projects") make the same list actionable on its own. The visual page does not suffer, since the claim sits immediately below each label. Fix: make the heading carry the claim and keep the type word as a labelled chip beside it.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The build does not serve the route the scenario specifies. The brief names /changelog/3.4.0 as the route; A's README instructs the reader to open the root URL and ships a single index.html at the package root, so the release is not addressable at a versioned path and a future 3.5.0 entry would have nowhere to live beside it. B places its page at /changelog/3.4.0/ with a root redirect. No content or behaviour is affected. Fix: nest the page under changelog/3.4.0/ and keep a root redirect.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The legend doubles as a five-link navigation block placed before any note, so keyboard users pass through Breaking, Changed, Added, Fixed, and Deprecated links before reaching the breaking note's own Copy and reference actions — verified in the tab order I collected from the live page. With only five notes on a single screen, these anchors add tab stops without shortening any real journey, and they partly duplicate the topbar's "Jump to breaking". Fix: keep the legend as a non-interactive key, or keep the links but move the block after the breaking note.

reviews.choice_reason: Both outputs surface the breaking retention change and the existing-project exception in one scan, keep a readable narrative, and stay within the supplied facts, so the decision turns on the required interactions and states, which I verified by serving both packages locally with Playwright. (1) A's states are honest and robust: with the clipboard blocked, A reports 'Couldn't copy — select the retentionDays value above instead', while B still displays 'Copied "retentionDays"' — a false success confirmation on the packet's central follow-up action. (2) A's 'Jump to breaking' clears an active search filter and moves focus to the breaking section (verified activeElement=section#note-breaking); B's jump silently fails while a filter hides the target — focus falls to body and the filter is not cleared. (3) A is static, progressively enhanced HTML (full changelog text without JS, live regions announce both copy state and the no-results state); B renders everything client-side (empty page without JS) and its zero-results state is never announced to assistive tech because the only live region is cleared exactly when the count reaches zero. B genuinely scans better — descriptive per-note headlines and a real config-reference placeholder page are strengths A lacks — but for a release engineer whose risk is a missed breaking change or a botched follow-up, verified interaction correctness and honest state feedback outweigh B's superior headline scanning.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Copy confirmation asserts success even when the copy fails. With navigator.clipboard unavailable and execCommand returning false, the button still switches to 'Copied' and the live region announces 'Copied "retentionDays"' (verified in a locally served run). The fallback's return value is never checked. A release engineer could paste an empty clipboard into relay.config.json work believing the key was copied. Fix: gate the confirmation on the actual copy result and show a failure message otherwise.

findings.label: B
findings.description: 'Jump to breaking changes' silently fails while an in-page search filter hides the breaking note: focus drops to body, the page does not scroll, and the filter is not cleared (verified: activeElement=body, breakingHidden=true). The primary rescue action of the page can no-op invisibly mid-search. Fix: clear the filter before focusing the target, as packet A does.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The no-results state is never announced to assistive technology. The only aria-live region (#search-status) is set to empty text exactly when zero notes match, and the visible no-results block is not a live region (verified). Sighted users see the empty state; screen-reader users hear nothing. Fix: announce the zero-result message through the existing status region.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The changelog is rendered entirely client-side from a JS module; without JavaScript the page body contains only the title text (verified: 21 characters of visible text vs. A's 1131). For a static release-notes page this sacrifices resilience for no functional gain.

findings.label: B
findings.description: At the required 390 px viewport there is a large blank band (roughly a screen-quarter) between the toolbar and the first note, and the search placeholder is clipped mid-word. In the no-results capture the custom 'Clear' affordance overlaps the input's native clear glyph ('×Clear'). Content is otherwise complete and readable.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Footer copy overpromises: 'See the configuration reference for the full set of relay.config.json keys' links to a placeholder page that immediately states the full reference is not included. The placeholder page also glosses retentionDays as 'overriding the default used for new projects', a scoping the facts do not state (the fact is unscoped: set retentionDays to retain a different period). Both are corrected or plausibly derivable in context, so I did not mark a material unsupported fact, but the footer promise should match the destination.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Evidence gap: interaction-01-jump-to-breaking-changes.png is byte-identical to desktop.png (matching MD5), so the packet contains no captured proof the jump interaction occurred; interaction-02 and state-01 are also the same file. I verified the unfiltered jump works by running the source, but the packet's own evidence does not demonstrate it.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Note headings are category labels only ('Breaking', 'Changed', 'Added'), not descriptive summaries. The key claim is bolded in the body, so the scan still works with five notes, but B's headline style ('Default artifact retention is now 30 days for new projects') answers the engineer's question faster. Fix: add a short descriptive headline per note under the category label.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The configuration reference is an in-page placeholder box; 'Open config reference' scrolls and focuses that box rather than leading anywhere. This is honest (it states no URL was supplied) and satisfies the required interaction, but the 'path to the related configuration reference' is shallower than B's dedicated placeholder page with a back link.

reviews.choice_reason: A ships fully static, semantic HTML (role=banner, role=search, labeled inputs, visually-hidden legend heading) so the release notes are present and readable even if JS fails, while B's entire page — including the dedicated config-reference route — is an empty <main id="app"> shell rendered only by app.js, a real resilience gap for a CI-adjacent tool. A's copy-to-clipboard handler checks whether the fallback execCommand actually succeeded and shows an honest failure message; B's fallback path always displays 'Copied' regardless of outcome. B also has a reproducible mobile CSS bug (.toolbar switches to flex-direction:column at max-width:480px while .search keeps flex: 1 1 14rem, so the 14rem flex-basis is applied along the now-vertical axis) that inserts a large blank gap before the breaking-change content on the 390px viewport, visible in three separate evidence captures. B does have a genuinely stronger config-reference destination (a real page that honestly discloses no migration guide URL was supplied, versus A's static in-page placeholder) and a clearer job-framing sentence, but these gains are outweighed by A's stronger resilience, honesty, and mobile correctness.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The changelog and the config-reference page are both empty HTML shells (<main id="app"></main>) with all content generated client-side by app.js. If JS fails to load or execute, the page renders nothing at all — no release notes, no breaking-change warning.

findings.label: B
findings.description: On the 390px viewport, .toolbar sets flex-direction: column while its child .search keeps flex: 1 1 14rem from the desktop rule; in a column flex context that 14rem flex-basis applies to height, not width, forcing the search control to occupy ~224px and leaving a large blank gap before the breaking-change content starts.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The copy-to-clipboard fallback (document.execCommand("copy")) does not check its boolean return value — the button always shows 'Copied' even when the fallback copy silently failed.

findings.label: A
findings.description: In two evidence captures (interaction-01, state-01), the sticky topbar renders a second time mid-page, overlapping the breaking-change callout. This is consistent with a known Chromium/Playwright interaction between position: sticky and full-page screenshot capture rather than necessarily a real scrolling-browser defect, but it is the only evidence supplied and is confusing as presented.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The five note types are differentiated only by a label chip and a 4px left-border color; the breaking note gets no extra visual weight (background tint, size) versus the other four, slightly undercutting the 'identify the breaking change in one scan' requirement compared to A's shaded, callout-boxed breaking treatment.

reviews.choice_reason: B better enables the stated job, with real reservations. The highest-consequence fact in this brief is that `atlas release plan` is safe and `atlas release apply` publishes; B makes that distinction structural — two side-by-side cards under step 3, one labelled 'Preview only', one 'Publishes — makes the release live', each colour-coded and each carrying its own command — whereas A carries the same distinction in small inline badges and a prose sentence inside a single stacked step, where a developer skimming under a five-minute budget can slide past it. B also puts the Node-22 remedy immediately after the three steps (callout plus a Troubleshooting section adjacent in document order), so the 'if blocked' half of the job is one glance away; in A, Troubleshooting is the last of six sections, roughly 2,600px down the page. B gives every command its own copy button, verified in source and by clicking through a locally served copy; A ships exactly one (install), so a developer must hand-select `atlas login`, `atlas login --device`, `atlas release plan`, and `node --version`. The reservations are material and cost B on the dimension scores rather than the choice: B's copy button reports success even when the Clipboard API rejects (confirmed by stubbing navigator.clipboard in a locally launched browser — button reads 'Copied', aria-label 'Command copied to clipboard', live region announces the same, while the fallback text selection is what actually ran), B keeps six sidebar links focusable off-screen at 390px, and B asserts a capability the brief does not supply. A is the more disciplined document — exact fact match, honest routing from its empty sections, correct copy-failure handling, section order matching the brief — but it is a flatter read that does less to protect the one decision that can fail destructively.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The copy-confirmation state reports success unconditionally. In source/app.js the catch branch performs a text-selection fallback and then falls through to the same code that sets data-state='copied', relabels the button 'Copied', sets aria-label='Command copied to clipboard', and announces 'Command copied to clipboard.' in the live region. I confirmed this by serving B/source locally and clicking the install copy button with navigator.clipboard.writeText stubbed to reject: button text 'Copied', aria-label 'Command copied to clipboard', live region 'Command copied to clipboard.' The supplied state-01-copy-confirmation.png shows the same condition — the command text is visibly range-selected (only the fallback path creates that selection) while the button reads 'Copied'. A developer whose clipboard is blocked pastes whatever was there before into a terminal, in a workflow whose stated consequence is failed releases. Fix: track whether writeText resolved and branch the label, aria-label, and announcement on it, as the paired output does.

findings.label: B
findings.description: At 390px with the menu closed, the sidebar is moved off-screen with transform: translateX(-312px) while remaining display:block and visibility:visible. Measured on a locally served copy at 390x844: the first nav link sits at x=-296 with width 279, and tabbing from the search input walks through all six invisible section links before reaching page content. Keyboard and screen-magnifier users lose the focus indicator for six stops (WCAG 2.4.3 / 2.4.7). Fix: add visibility:hidden (or display:none) to the closed state and remove it on open, or mark the links inert while collapsed.

findings.label: B
findings.description: 'Preview only — nothing leaves your machine' states a network-behaviour guarantee the brief does not supply; see unsupported_claims. Fix: use the supplied wording — previews files, version, and destination without publishing.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Sidebar order and document order disagree. The nav lists Get started, Guides, CLI reference, Configuration, CI, Troubleshooting (matching the brief's enumeration), but the sections render in the order get-started, troubleshooting, cli-reference, configuration, guides, ci. Clicking the second nav item jumps near the bottom of the page, and because an IntersectionObserver drives aria-current, the highlight moves non-monotonically while scrolling — it reads as a broken indicator rather than a reading position. Fix: either reorder the nav to match document flow or keep document order aligned with the listed sections.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The Guides and CI sections are dead ends: 'Task-based guides live here.' and 'Continuous-integration setup lives here.' Both promise content that is not present and offer no onward route, so a developer who follows either nav item under a five-minute budget spends a click and gets nothing. Fix: state what is not covered and point to Get started and the CLI reference, which is where the answers actually are.

findings.label: B
findings.description: Inside the two step-3 distinction cards, the copy button overflows its .code-block container — measured 2.5px on the plan card and 10.3px on the apply card at 1440px. The clipping is visible in desktop.png and state-01/state-02, where the apply card's 'Copy command' button is cut off at the card edge. It lands on the most safety-critical control on the page. Fix: allow the code block to wrap the button below the command at constrained widths, as it already does at 390px.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The page contains six h1 elements — one per section (Get started, Guides, CLI reference, Configuration, CI, Troubleshooting) — with step titles as h2 beneath the first. A screen-reader user navigating by heading level gets six co-equal page titles and no signal that Get started is the primary content. Fix: keep one h1 for the page and demote section titles to h2, with step titles as h3.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Only the install command has a copy affordance. `atlas login`, `atlas login --device`, `atlas release plan`, `atlas release apply`, and the two `node --version` blocks are plain <pre> with no button, so four of the five commands in the documented path must be selected by hand. This satisfies the required interaction but leaves the rest of the job slower than it needs to be. Fix: apply the existing copy-button component to every code block; the handler already resolves its target by id.

findings.label: A
findings.description:
The search no-results state is not announced. Verified on a locally served copy: typing a non-matching query renders

No results for "zzzq"…

into #search-results, which carries no role=status or aria-live (the page's only live region is #copy-status, bound to the copy button). A screen-reader user gets silence and cannot tell whether the search ran. Fix: give the results container role=status, or move the empty message into the existing live region.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Resizing from desktop to a narrow viewport leaves the sidebar expanded. initMobileNav collapses only on initial load and its resize handler expands when wide but never re-collapses when narrow, so after a rotation or window resize the section list renders inline over the content. A's own state-04-390-px-viewport.png shows this: the header and the full nav list sit mid-page across the CLI reference section, obscuring the first table rows. Fix: have the resize handler call setCollapsed(isNarrow()) in both directions.

findings.label: A
findings.description: The Guides and CI sections assert publication status the brief does not supply — 'Task-based guides aren't published yet' and 'This documentation set doesn't yet cover CI-specific setup.'
